**CI.** I have understood the meaning quite well, and I confess that all things accord very well. Therefore, it seems to me time to proceed to the next one.

### XV. TANSILO.

Here you see a serpent that languishes in the snow where a ditcher had thrown it, and a naked child burning in the midst of the fire, with certain other minute circumstances, and the motto that says, <term>IDEM, ITIDEM, NON IDEM</term> <gloss>The same, in the same way, not the same</gloss>. This seems to me more like an enigma than anything else; therefore, I do not trust myself to explain it fully. Yet, I would believe that it wishes to signify the same troublesome fate, which torments one and the other in the same way—that is, most intensely, without mercy, unto death—with different instruments or contrary principles, showing itself to be both cold and hot. But this seems to me to require a longer and more distinct consideration. **CI.** Another time. Read the rhyme.

confession of the Lord and the one God; for this joins minds to Heaven and creates a distance from the East, upon which the Lord is.

829. Since religion resides in the highest parts of a human being, and from these highest parts his lower parts live and shine, and because Muhammad is involved in their minds together with their religion, some Muhammad is always placed in their view. In order that they may turn their faces toward the East, upon which the Lord is, he is placed below the Christian center <note>Latin: *Meditullium*</note>. It is not the Muhammad himself who wrote the <term>Alcoran</term> <gloss>Koran</gloss>, but another who performs his duty; nor is it always the same one, but he is changed. Once it was a man from Saxony who, having been captured by the Algerians, became a Muhammadan. Because he had also been a Christian, he was induced several times to speak to them about the Lord, that He was not the son of Joseph but the Son of God Himself. Other Muhammads have succeeded this one. In the place where that representative Muhammad has his seat, a fire like a torch appears so that he may be known; but that fire is not visible to others than Muhammadans.

830. The Muhammad himself who wrote the <term>Alcoran</term> does not come into view today. I was told that in earlier times he presided over them, but because he wished to rule over all matters of their religion as God, he was cast out from his seat, which he had held under the Roman Catholics, and was lowered to the right side near the south. Once, a certain society of Muhammadans was incited by malicious persons to acknowledge Muhammad as God. In order that the sedition might be quieted, Muhammad was brought up from the lower earth and shown, and at that time he was seen by me as well. He appeared like those corporeal spirits who have no interior perception, with a face tending toward black, and I heard him speak these words, "I am your Muhammad," and soon he seemed to sink down.

831. Muhammadans are hostile to Christians primarily because of the faith of three Divine Persons and the resulting worship of three Gods—as many creators—and furthermore, toward the Roman Catholics, because of their genuflections before images. Therefore they call the latter idolaters and the former fanatics, saying that they make a three-headed God, and that they say "one" while muttering "three," and consequently that they divide Omnipotence, and out of one and of the One they make three; and that they are like fauns with three horns, one for each god, and all three together for one; and that they pray in this way, chant in this way, and sound forth from the pulpits in this way.

832. Muhammadans, like all nations that acknowledge one God and love what is just and do what is good according to their religion, have their own Heaven, but it is outside the Christian Heaven. The Muhammadan Heaven is divided into two. In the lower one, they live honestly with several wives, but from there, no others are raised into the higher Heaven except those who renounce their concubines and acknowledge the Lord our Savior, and at the same time, His dominion over Heaven and Hell. I heard that it is impossible for them to think that God the Father and our Lord are one, but that it is possible for them to believe that He rules over the Heavens and Hells because He is the Son of God the Father. This faith is among them, through which ascent into the higher Heaven is granted to them by the Lord.

833. The fact that the Muhammadan religion has been received by more kingdoms than the Christian religion can be a scandal to those who think about Divine Providence and at the same time believe that no one can be saved except one who is born a Christian. But the Muhammadan religion is not a scandal to those who believe that all things are of Divine Providence. These inquire where it is, and they also find it. It lies in this: that the Muhammadan religion acknowledges the Lord as the Greatest Prophet, the wisest of all, and also as the Son of God. But because they have made the <term>Alcoran</term> the book of their religion, and consequently Muhammad, who wrote it, has taken hold of their thoughts, and they pay him some worship, they therefore think little of our Lord. So that it may be fully known that that religion was raised up by the Divine Providence of the Lord to destroy the idolatries of many nations, it will be told in some order, but first concerning the origin of idolatries. Before that religion, there was idolatrous worship—

<summary>Swedenborg describes the nature of the Muhammadan afterlife, the representation of Muhammad among them, and how their religion serves a providential purpose in curbing idolatry while acknowledging the Lord.</summary>
<keywords>Muhammad, Alcoran, Divine Providence, afterlife, idolatry, Christian faith, Heaven, religion</keywords>

Clearly, the greatest part of diseases coming from celestial influence and from the astral impression of the firmament of the greater world does not wish to be cured by miscellaneous remedies, such as the arcana of herbs, minerals, or metals. Instead, the cure should be instituted through astronomical influence with those things that have an analogy to the greater and lesser worlds, in which there is a true magnetic power of the firmament and a celestial impression for resisting diseases from the firmament of the greater and lesser worlds, as appears in <term>Persicaria</term> <gloss>smartweed</gloss>, <term>Solidago maior</term> <gloss>greater comfrey/goldenrod</gloss>, <term>Dracunculus</term> <gloss>dragonwort</gloss>, and <term>Symphytum maior</term> <gloss>greater comfrey</gloss>.

If a disease or pain is brought on supernaturally through incantation or the magical impression of the ascendants, the effort to heal using the former three is useless. Rather, according to Paracelsus, one must proceed magically and supernaturally, and the evil must be repelled in turn by the same means by which it was brought. Otherwise, there is an influential attractive power in the said simples, and all things cure magically, astronomically, and magnetically by divine ordination, because medicine exists within them and man is a magnet. For just as the sun and the stars have the power of attracting humidity from inferior things, so too does man—by his innate magnetic attractive power, like a magnet of iron drawing in spirit in place of nourishment—and inferior things have the same power of attracting from the superior, as we see in the time of the plague, and these <unclear>at-</unclear>

Furthermore (which is more remarkable), the stars which have been called *Nebulae* <gloss>cloudy patches</gloss> by astronomers up to this day are groups of stars packed together in a wonderful way. From the blending of their rays, while each individual star escapes the keenness of our eyes due to its smallness or its extreme distance from us, there arises that whiteness which has hitherto been believed to be a denser part of the heavens, capable of reflecting the rays of the stars or the Sun. We have observed some of these; and we have chosen to append the star patterns <term>asterismos</term> <gloss>constellations or star groups</gloss> of two of them.

In the first, you have what is called the *Nebula* of the Head of Orion, in which we have counted twenty-one stars.

The second contains the *Nebula* called Praesepe <gloss>the Manger</gloss>, which is not just one star but a collection of more than forty stars: besides the Aselli <gloss>the Donkeys</gloss>, we have noted thirty-six arranged in the following order.

Furthermore, another property exists <margin>5</margin>: the greater terms have a difference between them equal to the lesser terms themselves, and accordingly, the difference between the differences differs from the lesser difference itself in a double ratio <note>a ratio of 2 to 1</note> when the terms are set out in a double ratio; but in a triple ratio <note>a ratio of 3 to 1</note>, the terms and the differences will have a difference twice that of the term below it; in a quadruple ratio, thrice; and in a quintuple ratio, four times; and so on indefinitely. <margin>4</margin> Geometric proportions occur not only in multiple ratios <note>such as 2, 4, 8</note> but also in all forms of <term>epimoric</term> <gloss>superparticular, where the ratio is (n+1)/n</gloss>, <term>epimeric</term> <gloss>superpartient, where the ratio is (n+m)/n</gloss>, and mixed ratios. The exceptional property <margin>15</margin> of this <term>mesotes</term> <gloss>mean</gloss> is preserved in all cases: in continuous proportions, the product of the extremes is equal to the square of the mean; in disjunct proportions or those with more terms—even if not continuous, provided they are even in number—the product of the extremes is equal to the product of the means.

<margin>5</margin> For an example showing that the property of this proportion is preserved in all relations—multiple of every kind, <term>epimoric</term> <gloss>superparticular</gloss> of every kind, <term>epimeric</term> <gloss>superpartient</gloss> of every kind, and mixed of every kind—it shall be sufficient and enough for us to use that method in which we constructed these ratios from equality.

<summary>Nicomachus explains the unique properties of geometric proportions, specifically how the differences between terms relate to the terms themselves. He demonstrates that the rule for products of extremes and means applies to all types of mathematical ratios including superparticular and superpartient forms.</summary>

<keywords>Nicomachus of Gerasa, geometric proportion, geometric mean, superparticular ratio, superpartient ratio, mathematical properties, ratios of equality</keywords>

This precipitated Mercury is uniquely praised and commended, and truly it excels greatly. The Mercury of Life <note>original: "Mercurius vitæ", also known as antimony oxychloride</note> or flowers of butter of antimony <note>original: "flores butyri antimonij"</note>, of which we spoke above, produces the same effect if 4 to 12 grains of it are administered for three full days in an extract of Hellebore and colocynth <note>bitter apple</note>; it most successfully expels the dissolved salt. Afterward, however, sweating and urination should be induced with a decoction of sarsaparilla, holy wood <note>original: "ligni sancti", also known as Guaiacum</note>, or asarabacca root <note>original: "radice asari"</note>, always adding spirit of Tartar or other diaphoretics <note>sweat-inducing agents</note> and diuretics, as discussed above. Especially useful is the addition of the secret remedy <note>original: "arcano"</note> of wormwood or blessed thistle. It must be noted, however, that the three-day administration of Mercury of Life in adults often tends to cause a prolapse of the anus, which afterward is rarely or even with difficulty healed. In treating dropsy <note>original: "hydrope", an accumulation of fluid in the body</note>, it is necessary that such purgatives be used right from the beginning of the cure; afterward, diuretics and hydrotics <note>fluid-expelling agents</note> should follow. Otherwise, a <term>hysteron proteron</term> <gloss>the cart before the horse</gloss> <note>original Greek: "ὕστερον πρότερον"</note> will have occurred here, and all the serum or water having rolled down to the kidneys and ureters, very stubborn symptoms often arise there afterward due to the heavy burden. Furthermore, in the preparation of the extract of black Hellebore root, it is safer to use wine itself instead of spirit of wine. The root should boil gently in the wine without much noise, and this must be done with fresh wine until all the essential power has been extracted from the roots. <meta>This page continues the description of Sisinnius, the Novatian bishop of Constantinople.</meta>

it was often his habit to avoid his own skill in debate. In his manner of life he was not simple, yet he practiced this expense with extreme self-control. He lived luxuriously, wearing white garments and bathing twice each day in the public baths. Once, when someone asked him why he, being a bishop, would bathe twice a day, he replied: Because I cannot manage a third time. On another occasion, while visiting the bishop Sergius, he was asked by one of Arsacius’s followers why he wore clothing unsuitable for a bishop, and where it was written that a priest should dress in white. He said: You tell me first where it is written that a bishop must wear black garments. When the questioner was at a loss for an answer, Sisinnius followed up his counter-question: You would not be able to show that a priest must dress in black. But Solomon advised me, saying, Let your garments be white <note>Ecclesiastes 9:8</note>. And the Savior in the Gospels is shown wearing white clothing. Furthermore, he showed Moses and Elijah to the apostles dressed in white. By saying these and many other things readily, he was greatly admired by those present. 

When Leontius, the bishop of Ancyra in Galatia, took away a church from the Novatians, Sisinnius went to him while he was staying in Constantinople and asked him to return the church. Leontius answered warmly and said to him: You Novatians ought not to have churches, for you do away with repentance <note>The Novatians held a rigorist view that those who fell away during persecution could not be readmitted to the church</note> and shut out the loving-kindness of God. When Leontius had said these and many other such harsh things against the Novatians, Sisinnius said: Truly, no one has ever repented as much as I have. When the other asked again how he had repented, Sisinnius replied: Because I saw you. 

Once, when John <note>John Chrysostom, the Bishop of Constantinople</note> was finding fault with him and saying that the city could not have two bishops, Sisinnius said: Indeed, it does not have two. When John became angry and said: You see that you alone are a bishop by your own will, Sisinnius replied: I do not say this, but rather that I am not a bishop in your eyes, though I am one in the ears of the people. John, becoming indignant at what was said, replied: I will stop you from preaching, for you are a heretic. To this Sisinnius replied gracefully: I would even give you a reward if you would relieve me of such great labor. John, softened at once by this answer, said: I will not stop your freedom of speech if speaking is a burden to you. 

Such was the readiness and grace of Sisinnius in his replies. To write and record all his sayings would be a long task. I have shown through a few examples what kind of man he was when he took up leadership. I say this: everyone knew him for his learning, and because of this, all the bishops in succession loved and honored him. Moreover, all the illustrious members of the senate cherished and admired him. Many books have been written by him, in which he used a refined style and mixed in poetic expressions. He was admired more for his speaking than for his writings. For there was such grace in his face, his voice, his bearing, his look, and his whole bodily movement. He was loved for these reasons by all religious sects, and especially by the bishop Atticus. So much for the matters concerning Sisinnius.

Suppose now that a person wishes, by means of a life annuity, to ensure for their heirs a capital payable at the end of the year of their death. To determine the value of this annuity, one can imagine that the person borrows this capital in the form of a life annuity, divided by unity increased by the interest rate, and invests it at perpetual interest in the same fund. It is clear that this capital will be owed by the fund to their heirs at the end of the year of their death; however, the person will only have paid, each year, the excess of the life interest over the perpetual interest. The table of life annuities therefore reveals what the person must pay annually to the fund to ensure this capital after their death.

Maritime insurance, insurance against fire and storms, and generally all establishments of this kind, are calculated according to the same principles. A merchant has ships at sea; he wishes to insure their value and that of their cargo against the dangers they may encounter. For this, he gives a sum to a company, which guarantees the estimated value of his cargoes and his ships. The ratio of this value to the sum that must be given as the price of the insurance depends on the dangers to which the ships are exposed, and can only be assessed through numerous observations on the fate of ships that have departed from the port for the same destination.

If the insured were to give the insurance company only the sum indicated by the calculation of probabilities, this company would not be able to cover the expenses of its establishment. He must therefore pay a larger sum as the price of his insurance. But then what is his advantage? It is here that the consideration of moral expectation becomes necessary. We understand that the most equitable game becomes, as we have seen previously, disadvantageous, because it exchanges a certain stake for an uncertain benefit. The radiance of all things—all of them were established by the teachers. **Rabbi Eleazar** spoke to Isaac: Who is the <term>deika katya</term> <gloss>broken-hearted or humble one</gloss>? Isaac bowed his head. Isaac was humble regarding his portion, Heaven forbid he should be angry, for his portion was not like the others. And behold, Isaac represents <term>Gevurah</term> <gloss>Strength/Judgment</gloss>, yet he is called <term>Chesed</term> <gloss>Mercy</gloss> when he is bowed down. For all Judgment is sweetened by Mercy, and Mercy is from the King. Wisdom inherits Mercy, for Mercy bows, and Isaac as Judgment is included in Mercy. Isaac bows before Mercy, for out of it comes harsh Judgment. And so it is above, this one from that one, and this one emerging from that one, until everything is known as one. They all depend on one another, and for all to be found as one, Heaven is needed forever and ever. **Rabbi Eleazar** recognized that there are no divisions when we see it as one, and one desire is in both of them to complete the whole, such as Jacob. This is what is written: 
> passing through from end to end <note>Exodus 26:28</note>

This proves the whole; for if you do not read it but from our side and from the other side, all is known. All things can rise in a single balance, not changing and not shifting, as it is written:
> I am the Lord, I change not <note>Malachi 3:6</note>

**Rabbi Yehuda** said: All these lights shine from one another and depend on one another. They are established as one whole, not to be separated. Whoever separates them by his own power is separated from the life of the worlds. **Rabbi Isaac** noted what is written:
> And I will give children to be their princes, and babes shall rule over them <note>Isaiah 3:4</note>

This refers to the "brazen-faced" <note>impudent</note> Cherubim. It is written, "He who sits upon the Cherubim," and it is also written, "And He rode upon a Cherub and did fly." "He who sits upon the Cherubim" refers to when the Divine Presence dwells in stability and support <note>this is when perfection is found</note>. "He rode upon a Cherub" <note>singular</note> refers to when the King is not settled on His throne. "Sits upon the Cherubim" refers to two. Woe to the world when one Cherub turns its face away from the other, for it is written:
> and their faces shall look one to another <note>Exodus 25:20</note>

This occurs when there is peace in the world. **Rabbi Isaac** said: We have learned, "The nakedness of a daughter-in-law or a daughter thou shalt not uncover." Woe to him who uncovers their nakedness. In this manner it is written of Jacob, "passing through from end to end." Thus is the portion of Israel with the Holy One, blessed be He; they are found in their adornments just as it is above, as it is written:
> Israel, in whom I will be glorified <note>Isaiah 49:3</note>

Come and see, **Rabbi Isaac** said: In former days, when one said to his fellow, "Show me one vessel and take money for it." Now a man says to his fellow, "Take money and show me a different thing," and there is no one to taste and no one to incline his portion, except for those few who are gathered and high unto the Holy One, blessed be He. As it is written:
> Thy people also shall be all righteous: they shall inherit the land for ever, the branch of my planting, the work of my hands, that I may be glorified <note>Isaiah 60:21</note>

Woe that the money is fulfilled and sustained. **Rabbi Isaac** said: Woe, for I see those who are circumcised, all those who are crowned by the upper knots, searching. Woe that it is fulfilled, for all those below depend on those above, woe. A window opens within a window, and they are renewed and prepared from the smoke for the order that rests upon them. And as in the Book of Concealment <note>Sifra Detzniuta</note>, it is proven: Woe above, woe below, and all of them rise in one balance. What is the fear of the Book? **Rabbi Hezekiah said**: These sections are all in the Great Palace and fill all the earth. **Rabbi Yehuda** said: All of them are thus, and even better than this. **The Rabbi said**: Woe to him who turns away and bows, and to him who did not ascend and bow to them in this way.

### The Parable of the Wheat

A parable of a man who lived among the fields and did not know the ways of the city dwellers. He sowed wheat and ate the wheat as it was <note>raw grains</note>. One day he entered the city, and they brought him a good fine bread. He asked, "What is this for?" They said, "It is bread to eat." He ate it and found it very pleasant to his taste. **The Rabbi said**: "This is made from what?" They said, "From wheat." Later they brought him cakes kneaded in oil. He tasted them and said, "And from what are these made?" They said, "From wheat." Later they brought him royal pastries made with honey and oil. He said, "And what are these delicacies made of?" They said, "From wheat." He said, "Truly, I am the master of all these things, for I eat the essence of all these, which is wheat." And because of that...

<summary>This page discusses the mystical unity of the Divine attributes, emphasizing that Judgment and Mercy must be balanced. It uses the Cherubim as symbols of cosmic harmony and concludes with a famous parable illustrating how the simple essence of Torah is hidden within complex layers of wisdom.</summary>
<keywords>Cherubim, Jacob, Isaac, Balance, Mercy, Judgment, Parable of Wheat, Sifra Detzniuta, Unity</keywords>

Whoever has a portion in the holy people must show greater faith than all others by welcoming the <term>ushpizin</term> <gloss>sacred guests</gloss> to rejoice in this world and the world to come. A person should make the poor rejoice, because the portion of food intended for those guests belongs to the poor. One who sits within the wholeness of faith and invites these supreme guests, the guests of faith, and gives them their portion, they all stand before him and say:
> **Do not eat the bread of a stingy man...** <note>Proverbs 23:6. The original Hebrew implies a "bad eye," referring to one who is ungenerous.</note>

It turns out that the table such a person prepared belongs to himself and not to the Holy One, blessed be He. Concerning him it is written:
> **I will spread dung upon your faces, the dung of your festival sacrifices...** <note>Malachi 2:3</note>

Woe to that person when those guests of faith rise from his table. Rabbi Abba said: All the days of Abraham, he would stand at the crossroads to invite guests and set a table for them. Now that they invite him <note>as a spiritual guest during the festival of Sukkot</note> along with all the righteous and King David, and people do not give them their portion <note>by feeding the poor</note>, it is the hardest thing of all. About this it is called:
> **Depart, I pray you, from the tents of these wicked men** <note>Numbers 16:26</note>

And they all go up and say: <term>Isaac</term> says:
> **But the belly of the wicked shall want.** <note>Proverbs 13:25</note>

<term>Jacob</term> says:
> **The morsel which you have eaten, you shall vomit up.** <note>Proverbs 23:8</note>

And all the rest of the righteous say:
> **For all tables are full of vomit and filthiness, so that there is no place clean.** <note>Isaiah 28:8</note>

> At the arrival of the clouds <note>the rainy season</note>, ten times the square root of a flock of swans flew toward Lake Manasa. One eighth of the flock flew away from the water's edge into a forest of land-growing lotuses. Oh young girl, three pairs of swans were seen playing with great passion in the water beautified by tender lotus stalks. Tell me the total number of swans in that flock. 3

**Word Order:** Oh girl! At the arrival of the clouds, ten times the square root of the swan flock went to Lake Manasa. One eighth part flew from the water's bank and reached the forest of land-growing lotuses. Three pairs of swans were seen enjoying play in the water adorned with young lotus shoots. Therefore, tell the entire number of the flock. 3

**Meaning:** Oh beloved girl of sixteen years! There was a group of swans. Among them, when the rainy season arrived, ten times the square root went to Lake Manasa. One eighth part of the total flew from the shore and went to a land-lotus forest. Three pairs <note>six swans</note> were seen playing with great affection in water shining with soft lotus roots. Tell me, how many swans were in that group? 3

**Statement of Problem:** <term>Mulaguna</term> <gloss>coefficient of the square root</gloss> is 10; <term>Ashtansha</term> <gloss>the eighth part</gloss> is 1/8; <term>Drishyam</term> <gloss>the visible/known quantity</gloss> is 6. Since the rule states "when increased or decreased by fractions," here we divide the known quantity and the square root coefficient by the remainder of one <note>1 minus the fraction 1/8</note>, which is 7/8. Dividing the known quantity 6 by 7/8 gives 48/7. Dividing the square root coefficient 10 by 7/8 gives 80/7. Half of this coefficient is 40/7. Its square is 1600/49. Adding this to the known quantity <note>after adjusting the denominator</note> results in 1936/49. The square root of this is 44/7. Adding half the coefficient <note>40/7</note> to this and squaring the result, the sum of the swans is found to be 144.

**Expansion:** According to the rule stated in the second verse, the eighth part <gloss>1/8</gloss> was subtracted from one, resulting in 1 minus 1/8 equals 7/8. This was used to divide the known quantity 6, resulting in 6 divided by 7/8, which is 6 multiplied by 8/7, equaling 48/7. This became the adjusted <term>drishya rashi</term> <gloss>visible quantity</gloss>. Similarly, the square root coefficient 10 was divided by 7/8, resulting in 10 multiplied by 8/7, equaling 80/7. This became the adjusted <term>mula rashi</term> <gloss>root quantity</gloss>. Now, treating 48/7 as the known quantity and 80/7 as the square root coefficient, the calculation was performed according to the method in the previous verse. Specifically, half of the square root coefficient is 40/7. The square of this is 1600/49. This was added to the known quantity 48/7...

III. First, it appears that a possessor in good faith (for a possessor in bad faith is held liable for more than the mere value of the object, due to his own deed) is not held liable for any restitution if the object has perished: because neither does he have the object itself, nor has he gained anything from it.

<margin>Medina on contracts, quest. 10.</margin>
IV. Second, a possessor in good faith is held liable for the restitution of even the existing fruits of the object: I mean the fruits of the object; for the fruits of one's own labor, even if they would not have been produced without the object, are nevertheless not owed to the object. The cause of this obligation arises from ownership. For whoever is the owner of an object is, by nature, also the owner of the fruits of that object.

<margin>Zeff. Bk. 2, ch. 14. Navar. ch. 17, no. 7.</margin>
V. Third, a possessor in good faith is held liable for the restitution of both the object and consumed fruits, provided that he would have consumed just as much in any other way: for in this respect, he is considered enriched. Thus, Gaius Caesar Caligula <note>original: "C. Cæsar Caligula"</note> is praised at the beginning of his reign because, to those to whom he restored kingdoms, he also added the fruits of the intervening time.

<margin>Suet. ch. 16.</margin>
VI. Fourth, he is not held liable for fruits he neglected to collect: because he neither has the object, nor anything that succeeds in the place of the object.

VII. Fifth, if such a possessor gives to another an object that was donated to him, he is not held liable unless he would have donated just as much even without this object: for then it will be a gain to have spared his own property.

<margin>Law "Quivaes," § last, D. "De furti."</margin>
VIII. Sixth, if he has sold an object he bought, he is not held liable, unless perhaps he sold it for more: but if he sold an object that was donated to him, he is held liable to restore the price, unless perhaps he squandered the price, which he would not have otherwise squandered.

<margin>Law "Si & rem," D. "De petit. hereditatis."</margin>
IX. Seventh, an object belonging to another, bought in good faith, must be restored, nor can the price expended be reclaimed. To this rule, it seems to me, an exception must be added: unless the owner could not have recovered possession of his property without some expense, for instance, if the object was in the hands of pirates. For then, the amount that the owner would have willingly spent can be deducted. Indeed, the very possession of the deed, especially when recovery is difficult, is something of value, and in this respect, the owner is considered to have become enriched after the loss of the object. And therefore, although the purchase of one's own object is not valid under ordinary law, the jurist Paulus <note>original: "Paulus Iurisconfultus"</note> says it is valid if it was agreed from the beginning that the possession held by another should be bought back. Nor do I require here that the object be bought with the intention that it be restored to the owner, in which case there are those who say that an action of <term>negotiorum gestio</term> <gloss>management of another's affairs</gloss> arises.

# AGAINST CELSUS IV 30. 31.

<margin>5</margin> Celsus says that the Jews were runaways from Egypt, who never performed anything noteworthy, and were never held in any account or number. Concerning their not being runaways, and that they were not Egyptians but Hebrews who had settled in Egypt as sojourners, we have already spoken in the previous sections <note>original: "III 5—8"</note>. If he thinks he can establish that they were of no account or number based on the fact that history concerning them is not readily found among the Greeks, we shall say this: if anyone were to dwell upon their original form of government <term>politeia</term> <gloss>civil constitution or way of life</gloss> and the arrangement of their laws, he would find that they were people who exhibited a shadow of a heavenly life upon the earth <note>Job 8:9, Hebrews 10:1</note>. Among them, no one else was recognized as God except the One over all, and no maker of images was a citizen. <margin>10</margin> For neither painter nor sculptor existed in their commonwealth, since the law expelled all such persons from it, so that there might be no pretext for the construction of images—which attracts the attention of foolish men and drags the eyes of the soul down from God to the earth. There was also a law among them to this effect: "Do not act lawlessly and make for yourselves a carved image, any likeness of a form, male or female, the likeness of any beast of those that are upon the earth, the likeness of any winged bird that flies under heaven, the likeness of any creeping thing that creeps upon the earth, the likeness of any fish, as many as are in the waters beneath the earth" <note>Deuteronomy 4:16—18</note>. And the law intended that, by dealing with the truth concerning each thing, they should not manufacture other things contrary to the truth, which give a false representation of the truly male, the truly female, the nature of beasts, the race of birds, or of creeping things, or of fish. <margin>25</margin> Also solemn and magnificent among them is the command: "Lest, looking up to heaven and seeing the sun and the moon and the stars, the whole host of heaven, you be led astray and worship them and serve them" <note>Deuteronomy 4:19</note>.

What a state of government <term>politeia</term> it was for a whole nation, among whom it was not even possible for an effeminate man <term>thēlydrian</term> <gloss>a man who has been feminized or a male prostitute</gloss> to be seen! <margin>30</margin> It is also wonderful that the fuels of youthful passion, the prostitutes, were removed from their commonwealth <note>Deuteronomy 23:17</note>. There were also courts consisting of the most righteous men, who had given proof of a healthy life for a long time <note>Exodus 18:21, Deuteronomy 1:15</note>.

<meta>The text contains Chapter 48 and the beginning of Chapter 49 of the Tao Te Ching, featuring commentaries by Su Zhe, Lü Huiqing, Huang Maocai, and Xizhai.</meta>

<margin><term>Su</term> <gloss>Su Zhe, 1039–1112 AD</gloss>’s Commentary</margin> Those who do not know the <term>Tao</term> <gloss>the Way</gloss> but devote themselves to learning will find that what they hear and see increases daily. However, without a single principle to unify this knowledge, they cannot avoid it becoming a burden. Confucius said: To hear much and select what is good to follow, or to see much and remember it, is only the second level of knowledge. If one day you know the Way, you will look back on worldly deceptions and see that nothing is not a delusion. Removing delusion and returning to one's true nature is what is called "decreasing." Confucius asked Zigong: Do you think I am one who learns much and remembers it all? Zigong replied: Yes, is it not so? Confucius said: No, I have one thread that runs through it all. To forget the mind in order to restore nature to purity is called decreasing. When delusions no longer remain and one reaches the point where even this forgetting is forgotten, nature is restored to purity without any remainder. Then one removes "doing" and does not fail to reach <term>Wu Wei</term> <gloss>non-action or effortless action</gloss>. Everyone has the desire to take hold of the world and manage its affairs, so they create activities and seek results. When this seeking mind is visible externally, things and people resist it, making success difficult. The Sage practices non-action and thus has no ulterior business in his mind. When this is visible externally, all things are at peace with him. Though he does not strive to take the world or manage its affairs, the affairs of the world follow him and are settled peacefully.

<margin><term>Lü</term> <gloss>Lü Huiqing, 1032–1111 AD</gloss>’s Commentary</margin> Practicing learning is for those who have not yet heard the Way. Because they have not heard it, their search must be broad, thus it is called "daily increase." Practicing the Way is for those who have already heard the Way. Having heard it, their practice must be nothing other than non-action, thus it is called "daily decrease." To "decrease and further decrease" refers to those who have not yet escaped the realm of "doing." One must even decrease the act of decreasing itself. Only then does one reach non-action. Non-action means being still and unmoving. "Nothing left undone" means responding and thus penetrating the causes of all things under heaven. Reaching non-action through the process of non-action is called the constant path. Learning without worry is called divine. The direction of the divine is what is called the Way. Who can attain such supreme divinity? From this we can see that winning the world is always done through non-action. If one resorts to "doing," it is clear that such a person is not fit to win the world.

<column-break/>

<margin><term>Huang Maocai</term> <gloss>A Song Dynasty scholar</gloss>’s Commentary</margin> Only after knowing everything can one speak of learning, therefore learning desires daily increase. Only after reaching the state where nothing is forced can one speak of the Way, therefore the Way desires daily decrease. However, increase can be sought through progress, while decrease is sometimes difficult to achieve through force. Only those of supreme clarity can suddenly cast off attachments and reach the realm of non-action. Thus they can leave nothing undone, and their practical application is inexhaustible. When applied to the world, they have more than enough room to maneuver.

<margin><term>Xizhai</term> <gloss>The scholar Li Zhicai</gloss>’s Commentary</margin> The purpose of learning is to seek knowledge, so it increases daily. The purpose of the Way is to remove delusion, so it decreases daily. If knowledge is not perfected, the decrease will not be complete. Therefore, daily increase serves as the foundation for daily decrease. If one decreases and further decreases until delusion is gone and truth is whole, then one reaches non-action. Upon reaching non-action, even when there is action, it has never ceased to be "non-action." This cannot easily be discussed in terms of mere increase or decrease. When non-action reaches its peak, despite the vastness of the world, a single thread runs through it. If one uses meddlesome activity to create more business, even a single object beforehand will become entangled and confused; how much more so the vastness of the world?

The Sage has no constant heart <note>or "fixed mind"</note>; he takes the heart of the people as his own. To those who are good, I am good. To those who are not good, I am also good. Thus, Virtue is goodness. To those who are trustful, I am trustful. To those who are not trustful, I am also trustful. Thus, Virtue is trust. The Sage dwells in the world with a cautious and merging mind; for the sake of the world, he makes his heart murky <note>meaning undifferentiated or simple</note>. The people all fix their ears and eyes upon him; the Sage <unclear>treats them all as his children.</unclear>

To the underworld spirits, pure from greed,
Choose by lot from the blood of the <term>Aepytidae</term> <gloss>the royal house of Messenia</gloss>,
A maiden to sacrifice in the night rites.
But if she is rejected at the slaughter, or by another, then 
Sacrifice another, given willingly for the slaughter.

When the god revealed this, they immediately cast lots among all the maidens of the <term>Aepytidae</term> lineage. The lot fell upon the daughter of Lyciscus. However, the seer Epebolus forbade her from being sacrificed, claiming she was not truly Lyciscus's daughter; he asserted that Lyciscus's wife, being unable to conceive, had secretly substituted the child. While Epebolus was explaining this, Lyciscus took the maiden and defected to Sparta. When the Messenians learned of Lyciscus's flight, they were disheartened. Then Aristodemus, a man of the <term>Aepytidae</term> house and more distinguished than Lyciscus in general reputation and military matters, voluntarily offered his own daughter for sacrifice. 

Human affairs and the determination of fate often hide such zeal, much like a pebble is hidden by the mud of a river. Even then, when Aristodemus was striving to save the Messenians, the following obstacle arose. A certain Messenian man (whose name they do not mention) happened to be in love with Aristodemus's daughter and was already about to take her as his wife. At first, he disputed with Aristodemus, claiming that since the father had betrothed her to him, he was no longer the master of the girl, and that he himself, as her betrothed, had greater authority. When he saw this was not succeeding, he turned to a shameless story: that he had slept with the girl and she was pregnant by him. 

Finally, he drove Aristodemus to such a point that, maddened by rage, he killed his own daughter. Afterward, he cut her open and proved she was not pregnant. The seer Epebolus was present and ordered that someone else must give a daughter, for the death of Aristodemus's daughter achieved nothing; the father had murdered her, but she had not been sacrificed to the gods whom the <term>Pythia</term> <gloss>the priestess of Apollo at Delphi</gloss> had commanded. When the seer said this, the Messenian multitude rushed to kill the girl’s suitor, believing he had brought a useless defilement upon Aristodemus and made their hope of salvation uncertain. 

However, this man was a very close friend of <term>Euphaes</term> <gloss>the King of Messenia</gloss>. Euphaes persuaded the Messenians that the oracle had been fulfilled by the girl's death and that what Aristodemus had done was sufficient for them. When he said this, all those of the <term>Aepytidae</term> lineage agreed that he spoke the truth; for their own fear for their daughters ceased, and each man was eager for the matter to end. Following the kings' advice, they dissolved the assembly and turned to sacrifices and a festival of the gods. 

When the Lacedaemonians <gloss>Spartans</gloss> heard of the oracle given to the Messenians, they too were disheartened, and their kings were hesitant to start a battle. In the sixth year after Lyciscus's flight from Ithome, the Lacedaemonians marched against Ithome, as the omens had become favorable to them. The Cretans were no longer present with them. The Messenians' allies were also late. The Spartans were already held in suspicion by other Peloponnesians, especially the Arcadians and Argives. The Argives intended to arrive secretly from the Lacedaemonians, and individually rather than by a common decree. The campaign had been openly forbidden to the Arcadians, and they also were not present. The fame of the oracle led the Messenians to risk battle even without allies. 

The events of the battle were mostly no different from the previous one; the daylight failed them while they were still fighting. It is not recorded that either wing or any company was forced back. They say they did not keep the formation in which they were originally drawn up; instead, the best men from both sides met in the center, and there the whole struggle took place. Euphaes, showing more spirit than was expected even of a king, recklessly attacked those around Theopompus <note>The King of Sparta</note> and received many fatal wounds. Fainting from loss of blood...

<summary>Aristodemus sacrifices his daughter to fulfill an oracle, despite a suitor's interference, leading to a continuation of the war between the Messenians and the Spartans near Mount Ithome.</summary>

Any passage that mentions the name <term>YHVH Elohim</term> <gloss>the Lord God</gloss> indicates actions performed through all the <term>middot</term> <gloss>divine attributes</gloss> which are completed through both the attribute of Justice and the attribute of Mercy. You find this, for example, in the creation of the first man, in his judgment, and in his expulsion. In all those matters, you find that they occurred through both Justice and Mercy, all in complete perfection, with Mercy and Justice applied exactly as required by true judgment. 

According to this principle, the Torah says: <note>Deuteronomy 32:4</note> The Rock, His work is perfect <term>tamim</term>. The explanation of the verse is this: The Rock who decrees judgment with strength does not act with cruelty. He does not decree judgment until His work is first "perfect" <term>tamim</term>, meaning the decree was first deliberated by the two attributes, Kindness <term>Hesed</term> and Justice <term>Din</term>. This is the meaning of "His work is perfect" <term>tamim</term>. 

The term <term>tamim</term> <gloss>perfect/complete</gloss> is a secret referring to two things. It is as if it said <term>te'omim</term> <gloss>twins</gloss>, except that the language of honor uses the term <term>tamim</term> for the two supernal things, while for things below it uses the term <term>te'omim</term>. Thus it says: <note>Exodus 26:24</note> They shall be twins <term>te'omim</term> from below, and together they shall be complete <term>tamim</term> at the top. Below they are twins; above they are "perfect" <term>tamim</term>. This is because below they appear as two separate things, opposites like an advocate and an accuser. But above, all is one intention. Whether it is the advocate or the accuser, both have one single purpose. There is no hatred or love there, nor is there any favoritism, but only true judgment. Therefore it says "His work is perfect" <term>tamim</term>, for He deliberated with Justice and Mercy and then decreed the judgment. This is the secret of true judgment. 

Regarding the phrase "For all His ways are justice," it means this is evident to the eye of every observer, as it is written: "For all His ways are justice." You already know that Justice <term>Mishpat</term> is comprised of both Judgment <term>Din</term> and Mercy <term>Rachamim</term>. This is because Justice corresponds to Jacob, who is the Middle Column, the one who mediates between the two "tents" of Abraham and Isaac. Abraham corresponds to Kindness <term>Hesed</term> and Isaac corresponds to Justice <term>Din</term>. Jacob balances between them, as he is called <note>Genesis 25:27</note> "a plain man <term>ish tam</term>, dwelling in tents." Justice <term>Mishpat</term> corresponds to Jacob, drawing from Kindness on Abraham’s side and from Judgment on Isaac’s side. Thus it says: <note>Psalm 99:4</note> "You have executed justice <term>mishpat</term> and righteousness <term>tzedakah</term> in Jacob." 

The Prophet also said: <note>Jeremiah 10:24</note> "O Lord, correct me, but with justice; not in Your anger, lest You bring me to nothing." The explanation of the verse "Correct me, O Lord, but with justice" uses the word <term>ach</term> <gloss>only/but</gloss> as a divider. It means: "with the half of the attribute of Justice which is Kindness." Since Justice is half judgment and half kindness, he said "but with justice." Then he added "not in Your anger, lest You bring me to nothing," revealing the secret of diminishing the half of Justice that comes from the side of Anger. 

Therefore, Justice <term>Mishpat</term> is dependent on Jacob, who is the "father" among the tribes. **And he answered.** "These are the four winds." This is like saying "for the four winds." Similarly, "and he came to Jerusalem" is like saying "into Jerusalem." Alternatively, it is like "white-black" meaning "towards white-black" and its equivalents. This refers to the division of the four chariots going out to the four winds of the heavens. This is to give permission to the four kingdoms to rule in the four winds, each one in its time. This refers to the whole world, which is a term for strength. "From standing before the Lord of all the earth." This means they act as messengers of God, who gave them dominion over this. It is like the verse, "the sons of God came to stand before the Lord." <margin>Job 2</margin>

**The one with.** "The black ones." He mentions the black ones first <note>referring to the second chariot in the vision sequence</note> because the era of the Babylonian kingdom had already passed. The kingdom of Media and Persia went first to the north country, for they were there to destroy it, and afterward they ruled over all the kingdoms of the earth. "And the white ones," which refers to the kingdom of Greece, "went out after them" once the kingdom was established. For Alexander of Macedon, the first king of Greece, killed Darius in Babylon and took the kingship from him and reigned; and afterward his successors ruled throughout the whole world.

**And the dappled ones went out to the south country.** These represent the Roman portion, because Rome is <unclear>shnunith</unclear>. This is proven by the Caesar who ruled over Rome; he began to fight against the Greek kingdom, and at the start of his wars, he went out to the land of Egypt, which is in the south. At that time, the Greeks were ruling in all lands. That Caesar prevailed over them, and he transferred the kingship from the Greeks and restored it to the Romans.

**And the strong ones.** These are a hint to the kingdom of Ishmael <note>The Islamic Caliphate</note> who incited themselves to seek kingship, to find a place that would be for <unclear>their power</unclear>. This is what is meant by "and they sought to go, to walk to and fro through the earth."

**And he said.** This means He gave them permission to walk about and conquer lands.

**Then he cried out.** Meaning, he called to me with a loud voice and said to me, **"See, those who go toward the north country have quieted my spirit in the north country."** This refers to the portion of the black horses that went out to Babylon to destroy it.

<margin>They use a water-vessel to signify the heart and the tongue of Egypt.</margin>
A divine water-vessel <note>original: "theia hydreia"</note> represents the sky and the earth gushing forth water. They liken the water-vessel to a heart that possesses a tongue. It is compared to a heart because among them, the heart is the ruling part of the body, just as the Nile stands as the ruler of Egypt. It is compared to a tongue because the tongue is always in a state of moisture and they call it the producer of what is good. They use two water-vessels, neither more nor less, because the operation of the Nile's rising is twofold. They assign one to the land of Egypt itself, since Egypt is capable of generating water on its own. They assign the other to the ocean, for from the ocean water arrives in Egypt at the time of the inundation. They also attribute the grain <note>possibly a misreading or reference to the harvest resulting from the rains</note> to the rains which occur in the southern parts of Ethiopia during the season of the Nile's rising. That Egypt itself generates the water can be understood from this fact: in the rest of the world's climates, the flooding of rivers is completed during the winter.

### Third Chapter.

Even when a suitor approaches them, women who are steady and bold must be tested. Because such women do not reveal their true feelings openly, the suitor cannot make a specialized approach; therefore, the examination of internal sentiments <note>original: "Bhava-pariksha"</note> is now described—
The suitor should examine the behavior of the woman; by observing her actions, her internal sentiment is examined. (1)

<note>Commentary:</note> Approaching her as one would a young maiden, he should examine her behavior, meaning her physical gestures and movements. For by examining these, her internal feelings are revealed. (1)

The author explains how such a woman is to be won—
If she does not disclose the secret matter, he should win her over through a female messenger. (2)

<note>Commentary:</note> If she does not disclose the secret <note>original: "mantram avrunanam"</note> means she does not openly reveal her desire for union. Because of her bold nature, he should win her over through a female messenger. (2)

If she rejects the initial approach but continues to associate with him, he should know that her mind is divided in two; he should win her over gradually. (3)

<note>Commentary:</note> If she rejects the approach made by the hero, but after some days have passed, she is found associating <note>original: "samsrijyamanam"</note> or moving in the hero's circles again, he should know her mind is divided. This is because she is in a state of testing herself, thinking, "I do not know what I should do." He should win her over gradually and not abandon her suddenly. (3)

If they lack the heart of a beast, even those with the physical form of a beast will be treated with affection. Traditions tell of creatures with horns, separated teeth, spread claws, those that fly above, and those that crawl below; these are called birds and beasts, yet they do not necessarily lack the heart of a human. Although they may have the heart of a human, they are treated with distance because of their appearance. <margin>These two points are agreeable</margin> <margin>Liezi: Yellow Emperor</margin>

<term>Paoxi</term> <gloss>Fuxi</gloss>, <term>Nuwa</term>, <term>Shennong</term>, and the Lord of Xia <note>Yu the Great</note> had bodies like snakes, faces of humans, heads of oxen, or noses of tigers. These possessed forms that were not human, yet they possessed the virtue of great sages. 

Xia Jie, Yin Zhou, Huan of Lu, and Mu of Chu had appearances and facial features <note>literally "seven orifices"</note> just like other humans, yet they possessed the hearts of birds and beasts. If the common people rely solely on outward appearance to seek the highest wisdom, they will never come close to finding it.

The <term>Yellow Emperor</term> <gloss>Huangdi</gloss> fought the <term>Flame Emperor</term> <gloss>Yandi</gloss> at the wilderness of <term>Banquan</term>. He led bears, grizzly bears, wolves, leopards, <term>pixiu</term> <gloss>fabulous fierce beasts</gloss>, and tigers as his front scouts, while using eagles, harriers, hawks, and kites as his banners. This was a case of using power to command birds and beasts. When <term>Yao</term> commanded <term>Kui</term> to direct the music, they struck and patted the stones, and all the beasts followed in dance. When the <term>Xiaoshao</term> music was played in nine movements, the phoenixes came to present themselves.

<summary>This passage argues that internal virtue and intelligence are independent of physical form, citing ancient sages with animal features and wicked kings with human appearances. From the meridian because the adjustment for the birth <note>referring to the calculation of the new moon or birth of the month</note> is easier with it than by working with horizons. The longest daylight hours for the latitude of Jerusalem <note>original: "Bayt al-Maqdis"</note> are fourteen hours and some fraction. The Jewish practice of using seasonal hours <note>term: "al-sa‘at al-zamaniyya" gloss: hours of varying length based on the duration of daylight</note> is only correct if the conjunction for the beginning of Tishrei <note>the first month of the civil year</note> occurs exactly with the autumnal equinox. However, it never occurs exactly then, but rather precedes or follows it by a significant amount as we have demonstrated previously. 

When we extract the time of the conjunction using the calculation provided by the Jews in the table which we analyzed according to their view, we then proceed to determine the start of the year and its quality—whether it is deficient, intermediate, or complete. We already have the knowledge of whether the year is an ordinary year <note>term: "basita" gloss: a year of twelve months</note> or a leap year <note>term: "kabisa" gloss: an intercalary year of thirteen months</note>. 

We then search the Table of Limits for a duration of weekdays whose boundaries contain the time we calculated for the conjunction. We look in the section for leap years if it is a leap year, or in the section for ordinary years if it is an ordinary year. When we find it, we will find alongside it the first day of the year in the week and its specific quality. Once we know the start of the year and its quality, and combine that quality with its status as an ordinary or leap year, we can determine the arrival of the following year's beginning.

> At the arrival of the clouds <note>the rainy season</note>, ten times the square root of a flock of swans flew toward Lake Manasa. One-eighth of the flock flew away from the shore of the water to a forest of land-lotuses. O girl, three pairs of swans were seen sporting with great desire in the water beautified by young lotus stalks. Tell me the total number of the flock. 3

**Prose Order:** O girl! At the arrival of the clouds, ten times the square root of the flock of swans went to Lake Manasa. One-eighth of the flock flew from the water's edge and went to a forest of land-lotuses. And three pairs of swans were seen engaged in the sport of play in the water which shines with young lotus stalks. Therefore, tell the entire number of the flock. 3

**Meaning:** O beloved of sixteen years of age! There was a group of swans. Among them, when the rainy season arrived, ten times the square root <note>of the total</note> went to Lake Manasaro-var. One-eighth of the flock flew from the edge of the water and went into a forest of land-lotuses. And three pairs of swans <note>totaling six</note> were seen playing very affectionately in water decorated with tender lotus stalks. So, tell me, how many swans were in that group? 3

**Numerical Setup:** The multiplier of the square root is 10; the fraction is 1/8; the visible amount <gloss>the remainder</gloss> is 6. As it was said <note>in the previous rule</note> that the values are increased or decreased by the fractions, here we divide the visible amount and the square root multiplier by the difference of the fraction from one <gloss>7/8</gloss>. The resulting visible amount is 48/7 and the square root multiplier is 80/7. Half of this multiplier is 40/7. Its square is 1600/49. Adding this <note>to the visible amount after adjustment</note> gives 1936/49. The square root of this is 44/7. Adding half the multiplier <gloss>40/7</gloss> and squaring the result, the quantity of swans is found to be: 144.

**Expansion:** According to the rule mentioned in the second verse, the eighth part <gloss>1/8</gloss> was subtracted from one, resulting in 1/1 - 1/8 = 7/8. This was used to divide the visible amount of 6, resulting in 6/1 ÷ 7/8 = 6/1 × 8/7 = 48/7. After applying the conversion of seven, 48/7 became the adjusted visible quantity <term>drishya rashi</term>. Similarly, the square root multiplier of 10 was divided by 7/8, resulting in 10/1 ÷ 7/8 = 10/1 × 8/7 = 80/7. After the conversion of seven, 80/7 became the adjusted square root multiplier. Now, treating 48/7 as the visible quantity and 80/7 as the square root multiplier, the calculation was performed according to the method mentioned in the verse above. That is, half of the square root multiplier was taken, which is 40/7. This was squared to become 1600/49. This was added to the visible quantity of 48/7...

III. First, it appears that a possessor in good faith (for a possessor in bad faith is held beyond the mere value of the thing due to his own action) is not held to any restitution if the thing has perished, because neither is the thing itself with him, nor has he gained from the thing.

<margin>Medina on contracts, q. 10.</margin>
IV. Second, a possessor in good faith is held to restore even the existing fruits of the thing. I say the fruits of the thing, for the fruits of industry, even if they would not have proceeded without the thing, are nevertheless not owed to the thing. The cause of this obligation is from ownership, for he who is the owner of the thing is naturally also the owner of the fruits of the thing.

<margin>Zeff. b. II. ch. 14. Navar. c. 17. n. 7.</margin>
V. Third, a possessor in good faith is held to the restitution of both the thing and the consumed fruits, provided that he would have consumed just as much otherwise, for in this he is considered enriched. Thus, C. Caesar Caligula is praised at the beginning of his reign because, to those to whom he restored kingdoms, he also added the fruits of the intervening time.

<margin>Suet. ch. 16.</margin>
VI. Fourth, he is not held for the fruits he neglected to collect, because he neither has the thing nor anything that succeeds in the place of the thing.

VII. Fifth, if such a possessor has donated to another a thing donated to him, he is not held unless he would have donated just as much even without this thing, for then the gain will be that he has spared his own property.

<margin>Law: Quivæs. §. last. D. on theft.</margin>
VIII. Sixth, if he has sold a purchased thing, he is not held, unless perhaps he sold it for more; but if he sold a donated thing, he is held to restore the price, unless perhaps he squandered the price, which he would not otherwise have squandered.

<margin>Law: if also the thing. D. on the petition of inheritance.</margin>
IX. Seventh, another's property purchased in good faith must be restored, and the expended price cannot be reclaimed. To this rule, it seems to me that this exception should be added, unless the owner could not plausibly have recovered possession of his property without some expense, as for instance if the thing was in the hands of pirates. Then it may be deducted how much the owner would willingly have spent. For the possession of the deed itself, especially when recovery is difficult, is something estimable, and in this, the owner is considered enriched after the loss of the thing. And therefore, although the purchase of his own property is not valid under ordinary law, Paulus the Jurist says that it is valid if it was agreed from the beginning that the possession, which is with another, should be bought. Nor do I require here that the thing be purchased with the intention that it be restored to the owner, in which case there are those who say that an action for the management of affairs <note>original: "negotiorum actionem"</note> arises.

# AGAINST CELSUS IV 30. 31.

<note>Celsus</note> says that the Jews were fugitives from Egypt, who never performed any noteworthy deed, nor were they ever held in any account or number. Regarding the claim that they were not fugitives, and that they were not Egyptians but Hebrews who had settled in Egypt, this has been addressed by us in the preceding sections. If <note>Celsus</note> thinks he can establish that they were of no account or number based on the fact that their history is not widely found among the Greeks, we shall say that if anyone were to dwell upon their original <term>politeia</term> <gloss>form of government or constitution</gloss> and the arrangement of their laws, he would find that they were men exhibiting a shadow of the heavenly life upon earth. Among them, no other God was recognized than the One over all, and no one who made images was permitted as a citizen. For there was neither painter nor sculptor in their commonwealth, since the Law expelled all such persons from it, so that there might be no pretext for the construction of images—an activity that attracts the attention of foolish men and drags the eyes of the soul down from God to the earth. There was also a law among them to this effect: "Do not act lawlessly and make for yourselves a carved likeness, any image in the likeness of male or female, the likeness of any beast of those that are on the earth, the likeness of any winged bird that flies under heaven, the likeness of any reptile that creeps on the earth, the likeness of any fish, as many as are in the waters beneath the earth." <note>Deuteronomy 4:16-18</note> Indeed, the Law intended that by associating with the truth concerning each thing, they should not fashion other things contrary to the truth, which give a false representation of the truly male or the truly female, or the nature of beasts, or the race of birds, or of reptiles, or of fish. Noble and magnificent was also their rule: "Lest, having looked up to heaven and seen the sun and the moon and the stars, the whole host of heaven, you be led astray and worship them and serve them." <note>Deuteronomy 4:19</note>

What a constitution it was for an entire nation where it was not even possible for an effeminate man <note>original: "thelydrian"</note> to be seen! It is also wonderful that the fuels for the passions of the young—prostitutes—were removed from their commonwealth. There were also courts consisting of the most just men who had given long proof of a healthy life.

<summary>Origen defends the Jews against Celsus's claim that they were insignificant Egyptian fugitives, arguing that the Mosaic Law established a unique, god-centered society that strictly prohibited idolatry and immorality.</summary>
<keywords>Origen, Celsus, Exodus, Mosaic Law, Idolatry, Aniconism, Constitution, Deuteronomy, Jewish history</keywords>

<margin>Su's Commentary <note>Su Zhe, 1039–1112, a prominent Song dynasty scholar</note></margin>Those who do not know the <term>Tao</term> <gloss>the Way</gloss> but devote themselves to learning find that what they hear and see increases daily. Yet, having no means to unify this knowledge, it inevitably becomes a burden. Confucius said: "Hear much, select what is good and follow it; see much and remember it; this is the second level of knowledge." If one day you know the Way, you will look back on all artificiality and false actions as nothing but delusions. To remove delusion and return to one's true nature is what is called "loss." Confucius asked Zigong: "Do you think I am one who learns much and remembers it all?" Zigong replied: "Yes, is it not so?" Confucius said: "No, I unify it all with one principle." Forgetting the calculating mind to purely return to nature is called loss. When delusion no longer exists, and one eventually forgets even this seeking mind to return fully to nature, then there is nothing left. Then one removes "doing" and does not fail to reach <term>Wu Wei</term> <gloss>Non-action or effortless action</gloss>. All people have the desire to take hold of the world and finish its affairs; thus they manufacture tasks and seek results. This intent is visible externally, and things resist it; therefore, difficulty arises and success is not achieved. The Sage practices Non-action and thus his mind is free of affairs. This is visible externally and things are at peace with him. Although he does not strive to take the world or manage its affairs, the affairs of the world follow him and find peace.

<margin>Lü's Commentary <note>Lü Huiqing, 1032–1111, a scholar known for blending Taoism and Buddhism</note></margin>Devoting oneself to learning is for those who have not yet heard the Way. Those who seek it without hearing it must be broad in their pursuit; hence it is called "daily gain." Devoting oneself to the Way is for those who have already heard it. Having heard it, one must act by simply doing nothing; hence it is called "daily loss." To "lose and lose again" means that one has not yet escaped "doing." One must even lose the act of losing itself. Only then does one reach Non-action. Non-action refers to being silent and unmoving. "Nothing is left undone" refers to being moved and subsequently penetrating all the causes under heaven. Reaching Non-action through Non-action is what is called the constant. Learning without worry is called "divine." The direction of the divine is the Way. Who but the most divine can participate in this? From this perspective, one always takes the world through Non-action. When it comes to "doing," it is clear that such is insufficient to take the world.

<column-break/>

<margin>Huang Maocai's Commentary <note>A Southern Song dynasty scholar</note></margin>Only after knowing everything can one speak of learning; thus, learning desires daily gain. Only after there is nothing one "does" can one speak of the Way; thus, the Way desires daily loss. However, gain can be sought through progress, while loss is sometimes difficult to achieve through force. Only the most enlightened can suddenly let go and drop everything, reaching the realm of Non-action. Thus they can leave nothing undone, and their practical application is inexhaustible. When applied to the world, they have more than enough room to maneuver.

<margin>Xizhai's Commentary <note>Referring to Li Daochun, a 13th-century Taoist master</note></margin>Devoting oneself to learning is the means to seek knowledge; therefore, there is daily gain. Devoting oneself to the Way is the means to remove delusion; therefore, there is daily loss. If knowledge is not ultimate, then the loss is not complete; thus, daily gain is the foundation for daily loss. If one loses and loses again until delusion is gone and truth is whole, then there is Non-action. Upon reaching Non-action, then even "having action" is never anything but "non-action." This cannot be easily discussed in terms of gain and loss. When Non-action reaches its ultimate state, though the things of the world are many, one unifies them. If one creates trouble by being meddlesome, even a single thing in front of one remains entangled and chaotic, let alone the many things of the world.

The Sage has no constant mind; he takes the mind of the people as his own mind. Those who are good, I treat as good. Those who are not good, I also treat as good; thus, virtue is goodness. Those who are faithful, I trust. Those who are not faithful, I also trust; thus, virtue is trust. The Sage is in the world, shrinking back for the sake of the world, making his heart turbid <note>meaning undifferentiated or simple</note>. The people all fix their ears and eyes upon him; the Sage <note>text continues on next page</note>

A girl untainted by the lower gods of the underworld,
Having fallen by lot from the blood of the <term>Aepytidae</term> <gloss>the royal line of Messenia</gloss>,
You must sacrifice in nocturnal slaughter.

When the god had revealed these things, all the virgins of the lineage of the <term>Aepytidae</term> immediately cast lots. The lot fell upon the daughter of Lyciscus. However, Epebolus the seer forbade her sacrifice, claiming she was not truly the daughter of Lyciscus; he asserted that Lyciscus’s wife, being unable to conceive, had secretly substituted the child as her own. While the seer was explaining the details concerning her, Lyciscus took the girl and fled to Sparta. When the Messenians fell into despair upon hearing that Lyciscus had escaped, Aristodemus, a man of the <term>Aepytidae</term> lineage and more distinguished than Lyciscus both in general reputation and in matters of war, offered his own daughter to be sacrificed of his own accord.

Human ambition is often thwarted by destiny, just as a pebble is caught in the mud of a river. Even then, as Aristodemus strove to save the Messenians, a sudden obstacle arose. A certain Messenian man (whose name is not recorded) happened to be in love with the daughter of Aristodemus and was soon to take her as his wife. At first, he disputed with Aristodemus, claiming that since the girl had been betrothed to him, the father no longer had authority over her, and that he, as her fiancé, had the greater right. When he saw this argument was not succeeding, he turned to a shameful lie, claiming he had already been intimate with the girl and that she was pregnant by him.

Finally, he provoked Aristodemus to such a degree that, driven mad by rage, the father killed his own daughter. Afterward, he cut her open and proved to all that she was not with child. Epebolus, who was present, then ordered that someone else must offer a daughter; he argued that the death of Aristodemus’s daughter had achieved nothing for the state, for the father had merely murdered her, rather than sacrificing her to the gods as the <term>Pythia</term> <gloss>the priestess of Apollo at Delphi</gloss> had commanded. When the seer said this, the Messenian multitude rushed to kill the girl’s suitor, believing he had brought a useless stain upon Aristodemus and made their hope of salvation uncertain.

However, this man was a very close friend to Euphais <note>the King of Messenia</note>. Euphais persuaded the Messenians that the oracle had been fulfilled by the girl’s death and that what Aristodemus had done was sufficient for them. As he spoke, all those of the <term>Aepytidae</term> lineage agreed that he spoke the truth, for their own fear for their daughters had ceased, and everyone was eager to agree. The people, following the advice of the kings, dissolved the assembly and turned from it toward sacrifices and a festival for the gods.

When the Lacedaemonians <gloss>Spartans</gloss> heard of the oracle given to the Messenians, they too were disheartened, and their kings were hesitant to begin a battle. In the sixth year after Lyciscus fled from <term>Ithome</term> <gloss>the Messenian mountain fortress</gloss>, the Lacedaemonians marched against Ithome, as the omens had become favorable to them. The Cretans were no longer present to assist the Spartans, and the allies of the Messenians were also late. The Spartans were already viewed with suspicion by other Peloponnesians, especially the Arcadians and Argives. The Argives intended to come secretly to help against the Lacedaemonians, acting privately rather than by a common decree. The Arcadians had been openly forbidden from the campaign, yet they also failed to appear. The Messenians were led to risk the battle even without allies by their faith in the oracle.

For the most part, the engagement was no different from the previous battle; the daylight failed while they were still fighting. It is not recorded that either wing or any single company was forced back. They say the ranks did not remain as they were first drawn up, but the best men from both sides met in the center, and there the whole weight of the struggle took place. Euphais, acting with more daring than was expected of a king, pressed recklessly against the troops of Theopompus <note>the Spartan King</note>, receiving many wounds, some of them fatal. Fainting from loss of blood...

Any passage that mentions the name <term>YHVH Elohim</term> <gloss>The Lord God</gloss> refers to actions performed through all the attributes, completed through both the attribute of Judgment and the attribute of Mercy. You will find this in the creation of the first man, in his judgment, and in his expulsion. In all those matters, you will find that they occurred through both the attribute of Judgment and the attribute of Mercy, all in complete perfection, with Mercy and Judgment applied exactly as is appropriate according to true judgment.

Based on this principle, the Torah states: "The Rock, His work is perfect" <note>Deuteronomy 32:4</note>. The explanation of the verse is as follows: The Rock, who decrees judgment with strength, does not act with cruelty. He does not decree judgment until His work is "perfect" <note>Hebrew: <term>Tamim</term></note>, meaning the judgment He decreed was first deliberated upon by the two attributes: <term>Chesed</term> <gloss>Loving-kindness</gloss> and <term>Din</term> <gloss>Judgment</gloss>. This is the meaning of "His work is perfect."

The term "perfect" <note><term>Tamim</term></note> is the secret of two things combined. It is as if it said "twins" <note><term>Te'umim</term></note>, but the language of honor uses the term <term>Tamim</term> for the two higher attributes, while for those below it uses the term <term>Te'umim</term>. Thus it says: "And they shall be coupled <note><term>Te'umim</term></note> beneath, and they shall be perfect <note><term>Tamim</term></note> above" <note>Exodus 26:24</note>. Below they are "twins," but above they are "perfect." This is because below they appear as two different things, opposites like a supporter and an accuser. But above, all is one intention. Whether it is the supporter or the accuser, both have one single aim. There is no hatred or love there, and no favoritism, only true justice. Therefore it says "His work is perfect," for He deliberated with Judgment and Mercy and then decreed the judgment. This is the secret of true justice.

As for the phrase "For all His ways are justice," it means this is evident to the eye of every observer. You already know that "Justice" <note><term>Mishpat</term></note> includes both Judgment and Mercy. Justice corresponds to Jacob, who is the Middle Pillar that mediates between the two "tents," which are Abraham and Isaac. Abraham corresponds to <term>Chesed</term> <gloss>Mercy</gloss> and Isaac corresponds to <term>Din</term> <gloss>Judgment</gloss>. Jacob decides between them, as he is the "perfect man, dwelling in tents" <note>Genesis 25:27</note>. Justice corresponds to Jacob, drawing from the Mercy of Abraham's side and the Judgment of Isaac's side. Thus it says: "You have executed justice and righteousness in Jacob" <note>Psalm 99:4</note>.

The prophet also said: "O Lord, correct me, but with justice; not in Your anger, lest You bring me to nothing" <note>Jeremiah 10:24</note>. The meaning of the verse "Correct me, O Lord, but with justice" uses the word "but" <note><term>Ach</term></note> to imply a division. That is, use only the half of the attribute of Justice that is Mercy. For Justice is half Judgment and half Mercy. Therefore he says "but with justice" and follows with "not in Your anger, lest You bring me to nothing," revealing the secret of diminishing the half of Justice that comes from the side of Anger.

For this reason, Justice is dependent on Jacob, who is the father of the tribes. Having known the great pain of children, when the Holy One, blessed be He, decrees against them, Jacob seeks mercy and righteousness for them. The secret is found in: "And the Lord of Hosts is exalted through justice" <note>Isaiah 5:16</note>. What is written immediately after? "And God the Holy One is sanctified through righteousness." This means when Justice is exalted, the harshness of Judgment rests and makes way for the attribute of <term>El</term> <gloss>God/Mighty</gloss>, which is the secret of the verse "And God the Holy One is sanctified through righteousness." In general, when the Lord of Hosts is exalted through Justice, the attribute of <term>El</term> comes from above and performs righteousness, and Justice is served. This is the secret of their saying that Justice is included in Mercy and Judgment, as it says: "You have executed justice and righteousness in Jacob."

The great secret is: "Righteousness and justice are the foundation of Your throne" <note>Psalm 89:15</note>. For "Righteousness" <note><term>Tzedek</term></note> is sometimes Judgment, according to how it is received in the flow of emanation, as I explained that <term>Tzedek</term> can be powerful judgment. But when Justice <note><term>Mishpat</term></note> is joined with it, the Throne is established in Mercy. If it is exalted through Justice and reaches until Mercy and Truth together, they are called the "Shining Countenance." Then everything becomes great Mercy, and this is the secret of "They shall go before

->Your face<-
