In the months of April and May of the year 1716, an abundance of haddock was brought into our city, which came to us from the seaside villages of Katwijk, Scheveningen, and Ter Heij. Many of these were still fresh, which we call <term>Krimp-schelvis</term> <gloss>a term referring to haddock caught and brought to market so quickly that the flesh is still firm and reactive</gloss>, and on some days they were so inexpensive that they were bought for less than a <term>stuiver</term> <gloss>a small Dutch coin</gloss> apiece. And such has also occurred some years ago.

Letting my thoughts wander regarding the multitude of these very tasty haddock, which were being caught with nets at that time, whereas they are otherwise caught with bait placed upon a fishhook; I imagined that there must be a reason why the small haddock approached our sea coasts in such abundance, since a month or two later, not a single haddock was being caught on our coasts.

I imagined that the abundance of the small haddock was dependent upon the bait, or food, that they were finding upon our sea coasts.

### Zechariah

For I have already seen the kingdoms, which are an allusion to the seven kingdoms <note>The commentator links the four chariots to various ruling powers in history</note>. And likewise: "What are these?" <note>referring to Zechariah 6:4</note> refers to the matter of my living among them.

And the angel answered and said to me, "These are the four winds of the heavens, going forth from standing before the Lord of all the earth. The one with the black horses goes forth to the north country, and the white ones go forth after them, and the dappled ones go forth to the south country." And the strong ones went forth and sought to go, to walk about through the earth; and he said, "Go, walk about through the earth." So they walked about through the earth. Then he cried out to me and spoke to me, saying, "See, those who go forth to the north country have quieted my spirit in the north country." <note>Zechariah 6:5–8</note>

**And he answered.** "These are the four winds." This is like "to the seven winds." Similarly, "and he came to Jerusalem" is like "unto Jerusalem." Another interpretation: "unto the son of Shachor" is like "to the son of Shachor," and similar cases. This refers to the division of the four chariots, and they go out to the seven directions of the heavens. This is to give permission to the seven kingdoms to rule in the seven directions, each one in its time, throughout the whole world, which is characterized by boldness. "From standing before the Lord of all the earth." This refers to the mission from God who gave them dominion over this, as it is written: "The sons of God came to stand before the Lord." <margin>Job 2</margin>

**The one with.** The black ones. He mentions the black ones because the time of the Kingdom of Babylon had already passed. The Kingdom of Media and Persia <note>historical successors to Babylon</note> went first to the north country, for they were there to destroy it, and afterward they ruled over all the kingdoms of the earth.

And the white ones, which are the Kingdom of Greece <note>the empire of Alexander the Great</note>, went out after them once that kingdom was established. Alexander of Macedon, the first king of Greece, killed Darius in Babylon and took the kingdom from him, and he ruled, and afterward his successors ruled throughout the entire world.

**And the dappled ones went forth to the south country.** This refers to the Roman portion, because Rome is <unclear>shnunith</unclear>. This is proven by Caesar, who ruled over Rome and began to fight against the Kingdom of Greece. At the start of his wars, he went out to the land of Egypt, which is in the south, and at that time the Greeks were ruling in all those lands. But Caesar prevailed over them and transferred the kingdom from the Greeks, returning it to the Romans.

**And the strong ones.** These are an allusion to the Kingdom of Ishmael <note>the Islamic conquests</note> who incited themselves to seek a kingdom, to find a place for themselves where they would have spirit. This is why it says, "and they sought to go, to walk about through the earth."

**And he said.** That is to say, He gave them permission to walk about and to conquer lands.

**Then he cried out.** That is to say, he called to me with a great voice and said to me: **"See, those who go forth to the north country have quieted my spirit in the north country."** This refers to the portion of the black horses that went out to Babylon to destroy it.

<summary>A commentary on Zechariah 6 interpreting the four chariots as the successive empires of Media-Persia, Greece, Rome, and the Islamic conquests. It identifies Alexander the Great and the Roman Caesars as agents of these shifts in global power.</summary>

They argue further: just as natural bodies are subject to celestial bodies, so too do artificial bodies, such as images, receive certain occult virtues following the influence of celestial bodies; therefore, artificial bodies, such as images, also receive some occult virtues from celestial bodies to cause certain effects, and thus it is not illicit to use them or others of this kind. Furthermore, demons can transmute bodies in many ways, as <term>Augustine</term> says in the third book of *On the Trinity*, and as is evident in those bewitched; therefore, it is permitted to use their power to remove those effects.

But in truth, the statements of all the holy doctors are to the contrary, and this has been made manifest here and there. Hence, to the first point, it is said that if natural things are applied simply to produce certain effects for which they are thought to have a natural virtue, it is not illicit. <margin>With this abundance they themselves in the middle make use of a heart and a tongue, according to the Egyptians.</margin>
A divine water-jar <note>original: "theia hydreia"</note>, or heaven and earth gushing forth water, is depicted by likening the water-vessel to a heart that possesses a tongue. They use the heart because, among them, this is the sovereign part of the body, just as the Nile is established as the sovereign of Egypt. They use the tongue because it always exists in moisture and they call it the parent of that which is good. There are two water-jars, neither more nor less, because the operation of the rising of the Nile <note>the annual inundation</note> is twofold. They assign one to the land of Egypt itself, since Egypt is capable of generating water on its own. They assign the other to the Ocean, for from it water arrives in Egypt at the time of the rising. They also attribute the grain to the rains which occur in the southern parts of Ethiopia at the season of the Nile's rising. That Egypt itself generates the water is possible to learn from this: in the rest of the regions of the world, the floods of the rivers are completed in the winter.

### Chapter 3

Even when an approach is made, women who are steady and bold must be examined. Such women do not reveal their true feelings openly, and therefore a specific method of approach is not used with them. For this reason, the testing of the disposition is now discussed:

A man making an approach should examine the behavior of the woman; through that behavior, her disposition is tested. 1.

<note>Commentary:</note> Approaching her as if she were a young maiden, he should examine her behavior, meaning her physical gestures and actions. Indeed, by examining these, her internal disposition is tested. 1.

How is she to be won? He says:

If she does not reveal the secret counsel, he should win her over by means of a female messenger. 2.

<note>Commentary:</note> Does not reveal the secret counsel means she does not disclose her feelings regarding sexual union. Because of her boldness, he should win her over through a female messenger. 2.

If she rejects the approach but continues to associate with him, he should know her mind is divided in two; he should win her over gradually. 3.

<note>Commentary:</note> Rejecting the approach means she refuses the advances made by the hero. If, after some days have passed, she is found associating with him, meaning she seeks the hero's company, he should know her mind is divided in two. This is because she is in a state of testing, thinking, "I do not know what I should do." He should win her over gradually and not abandon her suddenly. 3.

Regarding this, he states a specific detail:

If she rejects the approach but is seen again specifically adorned with ornaments, then in the same way...

<meta>This page is from the Yellow Emperor chapter of the Liezi, discussing the distinction between outward physical appearance and inward character or virtue.</meta>

If they lack the heart of a beast, even if they have the physical form of a beast, they will be treated with affection because of their appearance. Tradition says that those with horns, segmented teeth, spread claws, those that fly upward or crawl downward, are called birds and beasts; yet they do not necessarily lack a human heart. Conversely, even if one has a human heart, if their physical form is such, they may be treated with distance. <term>Paoxi</term> <gloss>Fuxi</gloss>, <term>Nüwa</term>, <term>Shennong</term>, and the Lord of Xia <note>Yu the Great</note> had bodies like snakes, faces of humans, heads of oxen, or noses of tigers. These possessed forms that were not human, yet they possessed the virtue of great sages. <margin>These two points are agreeable.</margin> Xia Jie, Yin Zhou, Lu Huan, and Chu Mu <note>notorious tyrants and failed rulers of Chinese history</note> were identical to other humans in their appearance and the seven apertures of their heads, yet they possessed the hearts of birds and beasts. If the masses rely solely on a single physical form to seek supreme wisdom, they will never come close to finding it. The <term>Huangdi</term> <gloss>Yellow Emperor</gloss> fought the <term>Yandi</term> <gloss>Flame Emperor</gloss> at the wilderness of Banquan. He led bears, grizzly bears, wolves, leopards, <term>pixiu</term> <gloss>fabulous fierce beasts</gloss>, and tigers as his vanguard, while eagles, long-tailed pheasants, hawks, and kites served as his banners. This is an example of using power to command birds and beasts. Yao commanded Kui <note>a one-legged mythical figure and master of music</note> to direct the music. When they struck and patted the sounding stones, the hundred beasts led each other in dance. When the <term>Xiaoshao</term> <gloss>the music of Shun</gloss> was played in nine movements, the phoenixes came to present themselves. <margin>Liezi: Yellow Emperor.</margin>

<summary>This passage argues that sagehood is determined by internal virtue rather than physical appearance, noting that ancient holy rulers often had monstrous forms while tyrants looked human. It also describes how the Yellow Emperor and Sage King Yao could command and influence animals through power and music.</summary>

Daiyu smiled and said, "Since you want to learn poetry, you must take me as your master. Although I am not an expert, I am capable of teaching you the basics." Xiangling laughed, "If that is truly the case, I shall take you as my master. You must not find me annoying."

Daiyu said, "What is so difficult about it that it should be a burden to learn? It is nothing more than the <term>Qi Cheng Zhuan He</term> <gloss>the four steps of a poem: introduction, development, transition, and conclusion</gloss>. If you truly have a remarkable line, you can even disregard the rules of tones and structure."

Xiangling laughed, "No wonder I often steal a look at one or two poems in old books; some are perfectly matched, while others are not. I have also heard it said, 'The first, third, and fifth syllables do not matter, but the second, fourth, and sixth must be distinct.' Now hearing you speak, it turns out these rules do not matter at all, as long as the wording is novel and extraordinary."

Daiyu said, "That is exactly the principle. The wording is ultimately a secondary matter; the most important thing is the <term>Liyi</term> <gloss>the initial conception or intent</gloss>. Xiangling said, "I only love <term>Lu Fangweng</term> <gloss>the poet Lu You</gloss> and his lines: 'The heavy curtains are not rolled up, keeping the fragrance long; the ancient inkstone is slightly concave, gathering much ink.' It is so vivid and interesting!"

Then read one hundred and twenty of Old Du's <note>the poet Du Fu</note> seven-character regulated poems, followed by one or two hundred of Li Qinglian's <note>the poet Li Bai</note> seven-character quatrains. Xiangling laughed, "I have indeed grasped something, though I do not know if it is correct. Let me tell it to you."

# The Reason We Established the Distance

We have established the distance from the point of midday <note>the meridian</note> because calculating the adjustment for a birth <note>an astrological natal chart</note> is easier by this method than by working with horizons. Furthermore, the longest daylight hours for the latitude of Jerusalem are fourteen hours and some fraction. The Jewish method of calculation using seasonal hours <note>hours of varying length depending on the time of year</note> does not function correctly unless the conjunction <term>molad</term> <gloss>the calculated time of the new moon</gloss> for the beginning of the month of Tishrei occurs exactly at the autumnal equinox. This never actually happens; rather, it precedes or follows the equinox by a significant amount, as we have demonstrated previously. 

Once we have extracted the time of the conjunction using the calculations provided by the Jews in the table we analyzed according to their views, we can then proceed to determine the start of the year. We can also identify the nature of the year: whether it is deficient, regular, or complete. We will have already determined whether the year is common <term>basita</term> <gloss>a regular 12-month year</gloss> or an intercalary <term>kabisa</term> <gloss>a 13-month leap year</gloss>.

We then consult the Table of Limits <note>the boundaries for determining the New Year</note> for a period of days of the week whose two endpoints encompass the time we calculated for the conjunction. We look in the column for intercalary years if it is a leap year, or in the column for common years if it is a regular year. When we find the correct entry, we will find alongside it the day of the week for the start of the year and its specific quality. By knowing the start of the year and its quality, and combining that quality with its status as common or intercalary, we can then determine the start of the following year.

**Prose Order:** O young girl! At the arrival of the clouds, ten times the square root of a flock of swans went to Manasa. An eighth part flew from the shore of the waters and went to a forest of land-lilies. And three pairs of swans <note>clarification: six swans</note> were seen intent on playful sports in water shining with young lotus-stalks. Therefore, tell the total number of the flock. ॥ 3 ॥

**Meaning:** O beloved of sixteen years of age! There was a group of swans. Among them, upon the arrival of the rainy season, ten times the square root went to Lake Manasasarovar, and an eighth part flew from the water's edge and went into a forest of land-lilies, and three (3) pairs of swans were seen playing very affectionately in water beautified by tender lotus-stalks; so say, how many swans were in that group? ॥ 3 ॥

Since it was said "when increased or decreased by fractions," here, by dividing the visible and the square root multiplier by one minus the fraction <gloss>7/8</gloss>, the results are: visible quantity <gloss>48/7</gloss>; square root multiplier <gloss>80/7</gloss>. Half the multiplier is <gloss>40/7</gloss>. The square of this <gloss>1600/49</gloss> is added <note>clarification: to the product of the multiplier and visible quantity</note> to get <gloss>1936/49</gloss>. The square root of this is <gloss>44/7</gloss>. Adding the half-multiplier <gloss>40/7</gloss> and squaring the result, the quantity of swans is produced: 144. ॥

Similarly, dividing the square root multiplier 10 by <gloss>7/8</gloss>, <gloss>10/1 / 7/8</gloss> = <gloss>10/1 × 8/7</gloss> = <gloss>80/7</gloss>. By dividing by seven, <gloss>80/7</gloss> became the square root multiplier. Now, taking <gloss>48/7</gloss> as the visible quantity and <gloss>80/7</gloss> as the multiplier, the operation was performed according to the method mentioned in the previous verse. That is, half of the square root multiplier is <gloss>40/7</gloss>. Squaring this <gloss>40/7</gloss>, it became <gloss>1600/49</gloss>. Adding this to the visible quantity <gloss>48/7</gloss>...

<margin>Sotol. IV. q. 7. art. 2. Covar. ad c. peccatum. par. II. §. I. Silv. in verbo <term>Restitut.</term> <gloss>Restitution</gloss> n. 3. quaest. 6.</margin> which are usually proposed by theologians instructing the internal tribunal of the mind.

III. For, in the first place, it is apparent that a possessor in good faith (for a possessor in bad faith is bound beyond the value of the thing by reason of his own act) is not bound to any restitution if the thing has perished: because neither is the thing itself with him, nor has he derived any profit from the thing.

<margin>Medina de contr. q. 10. Zeff. l. II. c. 14. Navar. c. 17. n. 7.</margin>
IV. Secondly, a possessor in good faith is bound to restore even the fruits <note>clarification: profits or yields</note> of the thing that still exist: I say the fruits of the thing; for fruits of industry <note>clarification: personal labor</note>, even if they would not have proceeded without the thing, are not owed to the thing. The cause of this obligation is from ownership. For he who is the owner of a thing, is naturally also the owner of the fruits of the thing.

V. Thirdly, a possessor in good faith is bound to the restitution of both the thing and the consumed fruits, if only he would have consumed just as much otherwise: for in this he is considered to have become richer. Thus C. Caesar Caligula <margin>Suet. c. 16.</margin> is praised concerning the beginnings of his reign, because to those to whom he restored kingdoms, he also added the fruits of the intermediate time.

VI. Fourthly, he is not bound for the fruits which he neglected to gather: because he has neither the thing, nor anything which succeeds in the place of the thing.

VII. Fifthly, if such a possessor has given to another the thing given to himself, he is not bound unless he would have given just as much even without this thing: for then it will be a profit to have spared his own thing. <margin>L. Quivas. §. ult. D. furti.</margin>

VIII. Sixthly, if he has sold a purchased thing, he is not bound, except insofar as he perhaps sold it for more: but if he sold a thing that was given to him, he is bound to restore the price, unless perhaps he squandered the price, which he otherwise would not have squandered. <margin>L. fi & rem. D. de petit. hereditatis.</margin>

IX. Seventhly, a thing of another purchased in good faith must be restored, nor can the price expended be reclaimed. To which rule there seems to me to be added this exception, unless insofar as the owner could not reasonably have recovered possession of his thing without some expenditure, as for example if the thing was in the hands of pirates. For then <margin>L. Sed & si lege. D. eod. L. Si eum servum. D. de rebus creditis. L. Mater tua. L. Si mancipia. D. de rei vindicatione.</margin> it will be possible to deduct how much the owner would willingly have spent. For the possession of the fact itself, especially when difficult to recover, is something estimable, and in this the owner after losing the thing is considered to have become richer. And therefore although the purchase of his own thing does not hold by ordinary law, yet the jurist Paulus <note>context: A Roman legal authority (Julius Paulus)</note> says that it holds, if from the beginning it was agreed that the possession which is with another should be bought. Nor do I here require that the thing be bought with the intention that it be restored to the owner, in which case there are those who say that an action of <term>negotiorum gestio</term> <gloss>management of affairs</gloss> arises. <margin>L. Sucr. D. de contr. emt. L. 1. D. de evittionibus. L. Si laborav. §. Si navis. D. ad legem Rhodiam. pern. v. quid de praedam ementibus. Aegid. Reg. diff. 35. dub. 7. num. 126. Host. tit. de a L. Si in emtione §. rei. D. de contr. emt.</margin>

Among them, nothing else was recognized as God except the one over all, and no one who made images lived as a citizen. For neither painter nor image-maker was in their commonwealth, the law expelling all such persons from <margin>15</margin> it, so that there might be no pretext for the construction of images—an activity which attracts the mindless among men and drags down the eyes of the soul from God to the earth. There was therefore among them a law such as this: "Do not act lawlessly and make for yourselves a graven likeness, any image, the likeness of male or female, <margin>19</margin> the likeness of any beast of those that are upon the earth, the likeness of any winged bird that flies under heaven, the likeness of any reptile that creeps upon the earth, the likeness of any fish, as many as are in the waters under the earth." <note>original: "μὴ ἀνομήσητε καὶ ποιήσητε ὑμῖν ἑαυτοῖς γλυπτὸν ὁμοίωμα..."</note> And indeed the law wished that they, by associating with the truth concerning each thing, should not fashion other things contrary to the truth, <margin>24</margin> misrepresenting the truly male, or the essentially female, or the nature of beasts, or the race of birds, or of reptiles, or of fish. <margin>Su's Commentary <note>context: Su Che (1039–1112), a prominent Song dynasty official and scholar.</note></margin>Those who do not know the <term>Tao</term> <gloss>Way</gloss> and yet devote themselves to learning will find that what they hear and see increases daily; yet, having no way to unify it <note>clarification: these observations</note>, they cannot avoid being burdened by it. Confucius said: "Hear much, select what is good and follow it; see much and remember it; this is the second level of knowledge." If one day one knows the <term>Tao</term>, one looks back at the false and the artificial; there is nothing that is not delusional. To remove the delusion and return to <term>xing</term> <gloss>nature/essence</gloss> is what is called "decreasing." Confucius said to Zigong: "Do you think of me as one who studies much and remembers it all?" He replied: "Yes, is it not so?" Confucius said: "No, I unify it all with one <note>clarification: principle</note>." Forgetting the mind to purely return to nature is called decreasing; yet if delusions still remain, one must continue until one also forgets this <note>clarification: very act of</note> forgetting. When the mind is pure and one returns to nature without residue, then one removes <term>wei</term> <gloss>purposeful action</gloss> and does not fail to reach <term>wu wei</term> <gloss>non-action</gloss>. All people have desires and the heart <note>clarification: or mind</note> to take hold of the world's affairs; thus they create business and seek things. Their heart is manifested outwardly and things <note>clarification: the world</note> loathe them, therefore they find difficulty and do not succeed. The Sage practices non-action and therefore has no business <note>clarification: or ulterior motives</note> in his heart. It is manifested outwardly and things are at peace with it. Though he does not <note>clarification: actively</note> take the world's affairs to act upon them, the affairs of the world follow him and are at peace.

<margin>Lü's Commentary <note>context: Lü Huiqing (1032–1111), a high-ranking official and reformer of the Song dynasty.</note></margin>To practice learning is for those who have not yet heard the <term>Tao</term>. Those who have not heard the <term>Tao</term> and seek it cannot help but be broad; therefore it is said: "it increases." To practice the <term>Tao</term> is for those who have already heard the <term>Tao</term>. Those who have already heard the <term>Tao</term> and practice it cannot help but practice non-action; therefore it is said: "it decreases." To decrease and further decrease means one has not yet avoided having <note>clarification: some</note> action. One must even decrease that which does the decreasing, and only then reach non-action. Non-action refers to being still and unmoving. "Nothing left undone" <note>original: "無不為"</note> refers to being stimulated and then penetrating the causes of all under heaven. To reach non-action through decreasing: this is called the Constant. Learning without worry is called <term>shen</term> <gloss>spirit/divine</gloss>. The direction of the spirit is what is called the <term>Tao</term>. As for the ultimate spirit, who can equal this? From this we see that taking the world is always done through non-action. As for those who use <term>you wei</term> <gloss>purposeful action</gloss>, we can know they are insufficient to take the world.

<column-break/>

<margin>Huang Maocai's Commentary <note>context: A Southern Song dynasty scholar and official.</note></margin>Only after there is nothing one does not know can one speak of learning; thus learning desires daily increase. Only after there is nothing one does not do can one speak of the <term>Tao</term>; thus the <term>Tao</term> desires daily decrease. However, that which increases can be sought through progress, while that which decreases is sometimes difficult to attain through force. Only those of ultimate clarity can suddenly drop <note>clarification: their burdens</note> and reach the realm of non-action. Thus they are able to leave nothing undone, and their applications are inexhaustible, acting upon the world with great ease.

<margin>Xizhai's Commentary <note>context: Li Zhichang (1193–1256), a Quanzhen Daoist leader.</note></margin>Practicing learning is the means by which one seeks knowledge, thus it increases daily. Practicing the <term>Tao</term> is the means by which one removes delusion, thus it decreases daily. If knowledge is not ultimate, then the decrease is not complete; therefore, daily increase is the ground for daily decrease. If one decreases and further decreases until delusion is gone and truth is complete, then there is non-action. As for reaching non-action, then in every instance of having action, there is nothing that is not non-action. This is not easily discussed in terms of decrease and increase. When non-action reaches its limit, though the world is vast, one unifies it with one <note>clarification: principle</note>. If one uses "having business" <note>original: "有事"</note> to create business, it is difficult to find leisure; even a single object before one remains entangled and confused, so how much more so for the vastness of the world?

The Sage has no constant heart <note>clarification: or fixed mind</note>; he takes the heart of the people as his heart. To those who are good, I am good; to those who are not good, I am also good; thus virtue <note>alternative: or "the power of the Way"</note> is goodness. To those who are faithful, I am faithful; to those who are not faithful, I am also faithful; thus virtue is faithfulness. The Sage is in the world, shrinking back <note>original: "惛惛"</note>, making his heart turbid for the sake of the world. The people all focus their ears and eyes upon him; the Sage <note>clarification: treats them all as children</note>.

After the god had revealed these things, they immediately cast lots for all the maidens who were of the race of the Aepytidae. The lot fell upon the daughter of Lyciscus. Epebolus the seer forbade them to sacrifice her, saying it was not necessary; for she was not <note>clarification: the daughter</note> of Lyciscus. He claimed the woman who lived with Lyciscus, since she was unable to bear children, had substituted the girl at that time. While he was explaining the facts regarding her, Lyciscus took the maiden with him and deserted to Sparta. The Messenians were discouraged when they learned Lyciscus had fled, but then Aristodemus, a man of the race of the Aepytidae and more distinguished than Lyciscus in general reputation and in matters of war, offered his own daughter to be sacrificed voluntarily. But human affairs, and especially zealousness, are often hidden by fate, like a pebble caught in the mud of a river. Even then, when Aristodemus was striving to save the Messenians, it brought about an obstacle of this sort. A man of the Messenians (whose name they do not tell) happened to be in love with the daughter of Aristodemus. At that time, he was already about to take her as his wife. At first, he entered into a dispute with Aristodemus, arguing that since he <note>clarification: Aristodemus</note> had betrothed her to him, he was no longer the master of the girl, and that he himself, having been betrothed, had become more the master than the father. Secondly, when he saw this was not succeeding for him, he turned to a shameless story: that he had slept with the girl and that she was pregnant by him. Finally, he provoked Aristodemus to such an extent that, driven mad by rage, he killed his daughter. Afterward, he cut her open and demonstrated that she was not with child. Epebolus, being present, ordered that someone else should come forward to give their daughter; for in his view, the death of the daughter of Aristodemus had gained them nothing. For he said the father had murdered her, but had not sacrificed her to the gods whom the Pythia had commanded. When the seer said such things, the multitude of Messenians rushed to kill the suitor of the girl, as one who had attached a useless pollution to Aristodemus and had made the hope of their salvation doubtful. But this man was a very close friend to Euphaes. Euphaes persuaded the Messenians that the oracle had its fulfillment through the death of the girl, and that what had been done by Aristodemus was sufficient for them. When he said these things, all those of the race of the Aepytidae said he spoke the truth; for the fear concerning their own daughters was ceasing for them, and each was eager <note>clarification: for the assembly to end</note>. And they, obeying the advice of the kings, dissolved the assembly; and from there they turned to sacrifices and the festival of the gods. The Lacedaemonians, having heard the oracle given to the Messenians, were themselves discouraged, and the kings were hesitant regarding both the future and the commencement of battle.

In the sixth year after the flight of Lyciscus from Ithome, the Lacedaemonians (for the sacrifices became favorable to them) marched against Ithome. The Cretans happened to no longer be present with them. The allies of the Messenians also arrived late. For the Spartans were already under suspicion by others of the Peloponnesians, and especially by the Arcadians and Argives. And the Argives intended to arrive secretly from the Lacedaemonians, and rather privately than by a common decree. The expedition was forbidden to the Arcadians openly. Thus they also were not present. For the expectation of the oracle led the Messenians to risk battle even without allies. A portion where it mentions <term>YHVH Elohim</term> <gloss>The LORD God</gloss> is performed through all the attributes that are completed by the attribute of Justice and the attribute of Mercy. For instance, you will find <note>clarification: this combination</note> in the creation of the first man, in his judgment, and in his expulsion, and in all those matters. You will find that they all came through the attribute of Justice and the attribute of Mercy, and everything was in perfect completion, with mercy and justice each according to what was appropriate in true judgment. According to this principle, the Torah said: "The Rock, His work is perfect" <note>original: "הצור תמים פעלו"</note>. The explanation of the verse is thus: The Rock who decrees judgment with strength does not act with cruelty; He does not decree the judgment except that "His work is perfect," meaning that the judgment He decreed was first deliberated upon by the two attributes, Kindness <note>term: Chesed</note> and Justice <note>term: Din</note>. This is the meaning of "His work is perfect" <note>term: tamim</note>. For the expression "perfect" <note>term: tamim</note> is the secret of two things, and it is as if it said "twins" <note>term: te’omim</note>, except that in the language of honor it uses the term "perfect" for two things above, and the term "twins" below. And so it says: "And they shall be twins <note>original: "תאומים"</note> from below... they shall be perfect <note>original: "תמים"</note> at its head." Below they are twins; above they are perfect. This is because below they appear as two things, a thing and its opposite, like a supporter and an accuser. But above, everything is a single intention; whether the supporter or the accuser, both have one intention, and there is no hatred or love there, and no favoritism, but only true judgment. Therefore it said "His work is perfect"—He deliberated with justice and mercy and decreed the judgment; and this is the secret of "true judgment."

As for what it said, "For all His ways are justice" <note>original: "כי כל דרכיו משפט"</note>, the explanation is that everything is <note>clarification: revealed</note> to the eye of every observer, as it says: "For all His ways are justice." You already know that Justice <note>term: Mishpat</note> is comprised of Judgment <note>term: Din</note> and Mercy <note>term: Rachamim</note>, for Justice corresponds to Jacob, who is the Middle Pillar that mediates between two tents, which are Abraham and Isaac. Abraham corresponds to Kindness <note>term: Chesed</note>; Isaac corresponds to Judgment <note>term: Din</note>. Jacob decides between them: "a perfect man, dwelling in tents." Justice <note>term: Mishpat</note> corresponds to Jacob, drawing from Kindness from the side of Abraham and from Judgment from the side of Isaac. And so it says: "Justice and righteousness in Jacob You have made." And the prophet said: "Correct me, O LORD <note>term: YHVH</note>, but with justice; not in Your anger, lest You bring me to nothing." Therefore, they say, when methods for restoring health are sought where exorcisms and natural medicines fail, it will not be illicit, if one sees it is vain, but if it were done where one wishes to procure health for oneself or another through images that are not <term>nigromanticas</term> <gloss>necromantic</gloss> and <term>astrologicas</term> <gloss>astrological</gloss>, or through rings and such things. 

Item, they argue: just as natural bodies are subject to celestial bodies, so also artificial bodies, such as images, obtain certain occult virtues following the hope of the influence of celestial bodies; therefore, also artificial bodies, such as images, obtain some occult virtues from celestial bodies to cause certain effects; therefore, to use them and others of this kind is not illicit. Furthermore, demons can transmute bodies in many ways, as <term>Augustine</term> says in book three of <term>De trinitate</term> <gloss>On the Trinity</gloss>, and it is evident in those bewitched <note>original: "maleficiatis"</note>. A divine pitcher <note>original: "Θεία δ’ ὑδρεία"</note>, or heaven and earth gushing water, they represent by a pitcher <note>original: "ὑδρεῖον"</note> resembling a heart that has a tongue. It is a heart because among them this is the ruling part <note>term: ἡγεμονικὸν</note> <gloss>sovereign or governing faculty</gloss> of the body, just as the Nile stands as the ruler of Egypt. It has a tongue because this is always in moisture, and they call it the producer of the good. They use pitchers <note>clarification: as symbols</note> which are neither more nor less <note>clarification: than two</note>, because the operation of the rise <note>clarification: of the river</note> is twofold according to them. They place one under the land of Egypt, because Egypt is of itself a generator of water; and the other under the Ocean. For indeed water arrives from this into Egypt at the time of the rise. They attribute the corn <note>clarification: the grain</note> to the rains, which happen in the southern parts of Ethiopia at the time of the rising of the Nile. That Egypt generates the water, it is possible to learn from this: for in the rest of the climate of the world, the floods of the rivers are completed in the winter.

<summary>This page explains the symbolic use of the heart and tongue within a pitcher to represent the Nile's flooding and Egypt's unique hydrology. It discusses the two sources of the inundation: the local Egyptian soil and the external influence of the Ocean and Ethiopian rains.</summary>

To the Chief Musician, a Psalm of David. May the Lord answer thee in the day of distress; may the name of the God of Jacob set thee on high. May He send thy help from the sanctuary and support thee from Zion. May He remember all thy offerings and accept thy burnt sacrifice. Selah. May He grant thee according to thy heart and fulfill all thy counsel. We will sing for joy in Thy salvation, and in the name of our God we will set up our banners; may the Lord fulfill all thy petitions. Now I know that the Lord saves His anointed; He will answer him from His holy heavens with the saving strength of His right hand. Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we will mention the name of the Lord our God. They have bowed down and fallen, but we have risen and stand upright. O Lord, save; may the King answer us on the day we call. And a redeemer shall come to Zion and to those who turn from transgression in Jacob, says the Lord. And as for Me, this is My covenant with them, says the Lord: My spirit which is upon thee, and My words which I have placed in thy mouth, shall not depart from thy mouth, nor from the mouth of thy seed, nor from the mouth of thy seed’s seed, says the Lord, from henceforth and forever.

And Thou art holy, inhabiting the praises of Israel. And one called to another and said: Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of Hosts; the whole earth is full of His glory. And they receive <note>clarification: the word</note> one from another, and say: Holy in the highest heavens, the house of His Presence <note>term>Shekhinah</note>; Holy upon the earth, the work of His power; Holy forever and to all eternity. The Lord of Hosts, the whole earth is full of the radiance of His glory. Then a wind lifted me up, and I heard behind me a sound of a great rushing: Blessed be the glory of the Lord from His place. And a wind lifted me up, and I heard behind me the sound of a great movement of those who praise and say: Blessed be the glory of the Lord from the place of the house of His Presence. The Lord shall reign forever and ever. The Lord, His kingdom stands forever and to all eternity. O Lord, God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, our fathers, keep this forever as the inclination of the thoughts of the heart of Thy people, and direct their heart toward Thee. And He, being merciful, forgiveth iniquity and destroyeth not; yea, many a time He turneth His anger away and stirreth not up all His wrath. For Thou, O Lord, art good and forgiving, and abundant in kindness to all who call upon Thee. Thy righteousness is an everlasting righteousness, and Thy Torah is truth. Thou wilt show truth to Jacob and kindness to Abraham, as Thou hast sworn to our fathers from the days of old. Blessed be the Lord day by day, who bears our burden; God is our salvation. Selah. The Lord of Hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our stronghold. Selah. O Lord of Hosts, happy is the man who trusts in Thee. O Lord, save; may the King answer us on the day we call. Blessed be He, our God, who created us for His glory, and separated us from those who err, and gave us the Torah of truth, and planted eternal life within us. May He open our heart through His Torah, and place in our heart His love and fear, to do His will and to serve Him with a perfect heart, so that we may not labor in vain, nor bring forth for terror. May it be Thy will, O Lord our God and God of our fathers, that we may keep Thy statutes in this world, and merit to live and see and inherit goodness and blessing for the years of the Messianic age and for the life of the world to come. To the end that my glory may sing praise to Thee and not be silent; O Lord my God, I will give thanks to Thee forever. Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord, and the Lord shall be his trust. Trust in the Lord forever and ever, for in Yah <note>term>Yah</note> the Lord is an everlasting Rock. And those who know Thy name will trust in Thee, for Thou hast not forsaken those who seek Thee, O Lord. The Lord was pleased for His righteousness' sake to magnify the Torah and make it glorious.

A prayer of David. Incline Thine ear, O Lord, answer me, for I am poor and needy. Preserve my soul, for I am pious; O Thou my God, save Thy servant who trusts in Thee. Be gracious unto me, O Lord, for unto Thee do I cry all day long. Rejoice the soul of Thy servant, for unto Thee, O Lord, do I lift up my soul. For Thou, O Lord, art good and forgiving, and abundant in kindness to all who call upon Thee. Give ear, O Lord, unto my prayer, and attend to the voice of my supplications. In the day of my trouble I will call upon Thee, for Thou wilt answer me. There is none like Thee among the gods, O Lord, and there are no works like Thine. All nations whom Thou hast made shall come and bow down before Thee, O Lord, and they shall glorify Thy name. For Thou art great and doest wonders; Thou art God alone. Teach me, O Lord, Thy way; I will walk in Thy truth; unite my heart to fear Thy name. I will thank Thee, O Lord my God, with all my heart, and I will glorify Thy name forever. For Thy kindness is great toward me, and Thou hast delivered my soul from the lowest nether-world. O God, the proud have risen up against me, and a congregation of violent men have sought my soul, and have not set Thee before them. But Thou, O Lord, art a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abundant in kindness and truth. Turn unto me and be gracious unto me; give Thy strength unto Thy servant, and save the son of Thy handmaid. Work for me a sign for good, that those who hate me may see it and be ashamed, because Thou, O Lord, hast helped me and comforted me.

O house of Jacob, come and let us walk in the light of the Lord. For all the peoples walk each one in the name of its god, but we will walk in the name of the Lord our God forever and ever.
May the Lord our God be with us as He was with our fathers; let Him not leave us nor forsake us. To incline our heart toward Him, to walk in all His ways, and to keep His commandments and His statutes and His judgments, which He commanded our fathers. And let these my words, wherewith I have made supplication before the Lord, be near unto the Lord our God day and night, that He maintain the cause of His servant and the cause of His people Israel, as every day shall require. So that all the peoples of the earth may know that the Lord is God; there is none else.

A Song of Ascents, of David. If the Lord had not been for us, let Israel now say: If the Lord had not been for us when man rose up against us, then they would have swallowed us up alive, when their wrath was kindled against us. Then the waters would have overwhelmed us, the stream would have gone over our soul. Then the treacherous waters would have gone over our soul. In explanation of that tradition of the Chosen One, peace be upon him: "Indeed, God Most High created the angels and placed intellect within them; and He created the beasts and placed lust within them; and He created the sons of Adam and placed within them both intellect and lust. So, he whose intellect overcomes his lust is higher than the angels, and he whose lust overcomes his intellect is lower than the beasts." The Truthful Messenger of God spoke the truth.

In the tradition, it is said that the Glorious Lord <note>original: "یزدان مجید"</note>
Created the inhabitants of the world in three kinds.
One group, in whom intellect, knowledge, and generosity prevail,
That is the angel; he knows nothing but prostration.
There is no greed or desire in his element,
Absolute light, living by the love of God.
Another group is void of knowledge,
Like animals [living] on fodder in <unclear>...</unclear>
They consider nothing but the stable and fodder;
They are ignorant of wretchedness and of honor.
This third kind is the son of Adam and human;
Half of him is a donkey, the other half inclines toward the sublime.
The donkey-half is inclined to the lowlands,
And this human is [made of] wind and contradiction.
Those two groups <note>clarification: angels and animals</note> are at peace from war and strife,
While this human is divided into three communities by the trial.
One group has become absolutely submerged <note>clarification: in God</note>,
Like Jesus, they have joined with the angels.
Delivered from anger, desire, and idle talk,
A human form, but in meaning, Gabriel.
Freed from ascetic discipline, piety, and struggle,
They have arrived [at the goal] from the lineage of humanity itself.
The other group has joined with the [beasts];
They have become pure anger and absolute lust.
That house <note>clarification: the body</note> was narrow, and that description <note>clarification: the divine attribute</note> vanished;
The Gabriel-like quality in them was [lost].
He made [it] dead, and the person who is without a soul
Is base, because of the soul that he does not possess.
He acts with a soul lower than the animals;
The deceit and trickery that he is able to weave—
The weaving of gold-embroidered garments,
Finding pearls in the depths of the sea,
With astronomy, the science of medicine, and philosophy,
He has no path to the seventh heaven.
For the pillar <note>clarification: of his knowledge</note> was the one that the ox held;
They named that "the mysteries of the universe,"
While its purpose is the preservation of the animal for a few days.
<column-break/>
He made his feet bound and [bound] his head;
He himself makes two feet into a head-bond.
His own act is [hidden] in that <unclear>...</unclear> and base one.
It is the explanation of the noble tradition:
When the Glorious Creator came to the secret,
He made the creatures evident in three kinds.
To one group He gave intellect and existence,
Who are the angels who perform prostration.
In their element, greed and desire do not exist;
They became the manifestation of the love of God.
He made one group void of knowledge;
They became entangled with animality.
Their knowledge is the stable and fodder;
They are heedless of wretchedness and lack of honor.
The third category was the human species;
They became capable of both good and evil.
Like the beasts, he has an inclination for the low;
The other half, like an angel, is of noble birth.
In humans, there is reaction between two opposites.
The human form became three communities, however:
The group joined to the ranks of angels, of angelic station,
Delivered from anger, desire, and idle talk.
Image them not as sons of Adam,
Those who are simple-hearted through piety and discipline.
The final category has the character of beasts,
Nothing but pure anger and absolute lust.
The house is narrow, that lofty description has faded;
The Gabriel-like quality has reached decline.
The person who is without a beloved first becomes dead;
The soul that is without the beloved is base and low.
The animal soul is far deeper in sorrow;
It performs every meticulous task for the world.
No other animal can act in such a way:
The gold-embroidered garment <unclear>...</unclear>
Drawing forth jewels from the depths of the sea.
Well-known philosophy, also medicine and astronomy—
There is no passage to the seventh heaven.
It pays attention to the ox and the donkey;
This attachment is worldly, from end to end.
This science of construction is tied to the manger;
The name of that fool is "the one who knows mysteries,"
Whose purpose is the preservation of the animal for a few days.

When the King finished the delicious morsels, he set the wine in motion and prepared a banquet of joy.
When the King had drunk two or three goblets of wine, perspiration rose from his rose-colored forehead.
He said: "O host of the golden palace, your dwelling is pleasant and your provisions are ample.
But these sixty steps of this high palace, over whose head the sky passes like a lasso—
Since sixty years have passed for you, how can you trample them under your feet?"
The host said: "May the King remain forever; may <term>Kawsar</term> <gloss>the celestial river</gloss> be his wine and the <term>Houri</term> <gloss>heavenly maiden</gloss> his cupbearer.
This is no wonder for me, for I am a man; how should I grow weary from such a staircase?
The wonder is that there is a daughter like the moon, soft and delicate like the King's silk and ermine.
A mountain-like ox upon her neck, she brings it to the place of feeding.
She climbs the sixty steps in one go, so that she does not rest at any step.
An ox, and what an ox! Like an elephant; a milch-cow does not pull its own fat <note>clarification: the ox is exceptionally heavy</note>.
By God, if anyone in this land could lift it even a breath's width from the ground!
A woman then, to the sixty-step fortress, carrying it up—how is this work not a marvel?"
When the officer told this tale to the King, he pressed his fingertip beneath his teeth <note>clarification: a gesture of amazement</note>.
He said: "How can a deed be of this kind? It could not be, and if it is, it must be sorcery.
I will not believe this speech as truth until I first see it with my own eyes."
And then he requested of the host to make the claim of his speech come true.
The host, having heard this, went down; he told the lion's tale to the ox-carrier <note>context: the "lion" refers to the King, and the "ox-carrier" refers to the girl, Fitna</note>.

It is said that after Xiangling met everyone and ate the evening meal, Baochai and the others all went to Lady Wang's <note>clarification: Aunt Wang's</note> place. Xiangling went by herself to the潇湘館 <term>Xiaoxiang Guan</term> <gloss>Naiad's House</gloss>. At this time Daiyu was more than half recovered. Seeing that Xiangling had also come into the garden to live, she was naturally happy. Xiangling said with a smile: "Now that I have come in, I have some free time. If you would teach me to compose poetry, it would be my great good fortune!" Daiyu smiled and said: "Since you want to learn to compose poetry, you must take me as your master. Although I am not fully proficient, I can generally manage to teach you." Xiangling smiled: "If it is truly so, I shall take you as my master; you must not get tired of me." Daiyu said: "What is so difficult about it that it is worth such concern? It is no more than the opening, the development, the transition, and the conclusion <note>original: "起承轉合" (qi cheng zhuan he)</note>. Within the development and transition, there are two pairs of couplets: level tones against oblique tones, empty words against solid words, and solid words against empty words. If one truly has a miraculous line, it is permissible even if the tones and categories do not match."

Xiangling smiled: "No wonder I often take an old book of poems to steal a look at a few, and find some are perfectly matched while others are not. I have also heard it said, 'The first, third, and fifth syllables do not matter, but the second, fourth, and sixth must be distinct.' Looking at the poems of the ancients, some follow this and some are wrong on the second, fourth, and sixth. I have been in doubt every day. Now hearing you speak, it turns out these rules are actually of no consequence, as long as the phrasing is novel and extraordinary." Daiyu said: "That is exactly the principle. Phrasing is, after all, a secondary matter; first and foremost, the 'conception' <note>original: "立意" (li yi)</note> is vital. If the intent and interest are genuine, then the poem is naturally good even without polished phrasing. This is called 'not letting the words damage the intent' <note>original: "不為辭害意" (bu wei ci hai yi)</note>."

Xiangling said: "I only love Lu Fangweng's <note>context: Lu You (1125–1210), a famous Southern Song dynasty poet</note> 'Heavy curtains unrolled keep the fragrance long; an old inkstone slightly concave gathers much ink.' It is described so vividly and interestingly!" Daiyu said: "Because you do not know poetry, you see these shallow and accessible lines and love them. Once you enter that pattern, you will never be able to learn your way out. Just listen to me: if you truly want to learn, I have the *Complete Works of Wang Mojie* <note>context: Wang Wei (699–759), a Tang dynasty poet and painter</note> here. You should first carefully study and master one hundred of his five-character regulated poems. Then read one hundred and twenty of Old Du's <note>context: Du Fu (712–770), the "Poet Sage" of the Tang dynasty</note> seven-character regulated poems. Next, read one or two hundred of Li Qinglian's <note>context: Li Bai (701–762), the "Poet Immortal" of the Tang dynasty</note> seven-character quatrains. Once you have these three people as a foundation in your belly, then take a look at Tao Yuanming, Ying, Liu, Xie, Ruan, Yu, Bao, and the others. You are such an extremely clever and sharp person; in less than a year's work, you need not worry about not being a master poet!" Hearing this, Xiangling smiled: "In that case, good Miss, take that book out for me, and I will take it back to read a few poems at night." Hearing this, Daiyu ordered Zijuan to bring the five-character regulated poems of Wang the Right Vice-President <note>context: An official title for Wang Wei</note> and handed them to Xiangling, saying: "Only look at those with red circles; those are the ones I have selected. Read them one by one. If there is anything you do not understand, ask your mistress <note>clarification: Baochai</note>; or if you meet me, I will explain it to you."

Xiangling took the poems and returned to the 蘅蕪院 <term>Hengwu Yuan</term> <gloss>Alcaic Enclosure</gloss>. She ignored everything else and simply began to read them one by one under the lamp. Baochai urged her several times to go to sleep, but she would not. Seeing her such painstaking dedication, Baochai could only let her be.

One day, just as Daiyu had finished washing and combing, she saw Xiangling beaming as she brought the book back, wanting to exchange it for the poems of Du <note>clarification: Du Fu</note>. Daiyu smiled: "How many poems do you remember in total?" Xiangling smiled: "I have read all of those selected with red circles." Daiyu said: "Have you grasped some of the meaning?" Xiangling smiled: "I have indeed grasped some, but I do not know if I am right. Let me tell you about it."

Therefore, the Jewish method using seasonal hours <note>term>الساعات الزمانية</note> <gloss>hours that vary in length based on the day's duration</gloss> does not function correctly unless the conjunction <note>term>الاجتماع</note> <gloss>the syzygy or new moon</gloss> for the beginning of <term>Tishrei</term> <gloss>the first month of the Hebrew calendar</gloss> happens to coincide with the autumnal equinox <note>original: "الاعتدال الخريفي"</note>. It never actually coincides with it; rather, it precedes or follows it by a significant amount, as we demonstrated previously.

When we extract the time of conjunction using the calculation provided by the Jews in the table which we analyzed according to their opinion, we proceed from that to the knowledge of the first day of the year and the determination of its quality—whether it is deficient, regular, or complete. We already have the prior knowledge of whether the year is ordinary <note>term>بسيطة</note> <gloss>a 12-month lunar year</gloss> or leap <note>term>كبيسة</note> <gloss>a 13-month embolismic year</gloss>.

We then seek, within the table of limits <note>original: "جدول الحدود"</note>, a duration of weekdays whose two boundaries encompass the time of conjunction we derived. We look on the side for leap years if it is a leap year, and on the side for ordinary years if it is ordinary. When we find it, we will find adjacent to it the first day of the year in the week and its quality. Once we know the first day of the year and its quality, and combine that quality with its status as ordinary or leap, we learn from this the occurrence of the first day of the following year.

As Leontius spoke these and many other such harsh words against the Novatians, Sisinnius said, "Truly, no one has ever repented as much as I have." When the other asked again, "How have you repented?" Sisinnius answered, "In that I have seen you." 

Once, when Bishop John <note>context: John Chrysostom, Archbishop of Constantinople.</note> was reproaching him for something and said that the city could not have two bishops, Sisinnius said, "Indeed, it does not." When John became angry and said, "You see that you claim to be the only bishop in your own opinion," Sisinnius replied, "I do not say that, but that I am not a bishop only in your ears, as I am to the ears of others." John, becoming indignant at what was said, said, "I shall stop you from speaking in public, for you are a heretic." To this Sisinnius wittily replied, "I would even give you a reward if you would relieve me of such great labor." John, softened by this response, said, "I will not stop you from your freedom of speech if speaking so completely grieves you." 

Such was the readiness and grace of Sisinnius in his responses. It would be a long task to write and record all his spoken words. Therefore, I have shown by these few examples what kind of man he was, having thought it right to govern. I say this: everyone knows him for his education, and because of it, all the bishops in succession loved and honored him. Moreover, all the prominent members of the Senate cherished and admired him. For there was such grace in his face, his voice, his posture, his look, and in the whole movement of his body. He was loved for these reasons by all religions, and especially by Bishop Atticus. > Ten times the square root of a flock of swans flew to Lake <term>Manasa</term> <gloss>a sacred lake in the Himalayas</gloss> at the arrival of the clouds. One-eighth of them flew from the water's edge to a forest of land-lilies. O young girl, three pairs of swans were seen playing with great joy in water adorned with tender lotus-stalks. Tell me the total number of the flock? ॥ 3 ॥

**Prose Order:** O girl! At the arrival of the clouds, ten times the square root of a flock of swans went to Lake <term>Manasa</term>. One-eighth part flew from the shore of the water and went to a forest of land-lilies. Three pairs of swans were seen eagerly engaged in play in water shining with young lotus-stalks. Then, tell the total number of the flock. ॥ 3 ॥

**Meaning:** O my dear sixteen-year-old beloved! There was a flock of swans. From among them, as the rainy season arrived, ten times the square root <note>original: "मूलदशकं"</note> went to Lake <term>Manasa</term>, and an eighth part flew from the edge of the water to a forest of land-lilies. If three pairs of swans—that is, six—were seen playing with great affection in water beautiful with soft lotus-stems, then say how many swans were in that group? ॥ 3 ॥

**Statement of Numerical Values:**
Multiplied square root: 10; Eighth part: <gloss>1/8</gloss>; Visible quantity <note>original: "दृश्यम्"</note>: <gloss>6</gloss>.
As stated by the rule "when decreased or increased by parts," we divide the visible quantity and the square root multiplier by one minus the fraction <gloss>7/8</gloss>. The visible quantity becomes <gloss>48/7</gloss> and the square root multiplier becomes <gloss>80/7</gloss>. Half of the multiplier is <gloss>40/7</gloss>. Its square <gloss>1600/49</gloss> added <note>clarification: to the product of the visible quantity and 1</note> gives <gloss>1936/49</gloss>. The square root of this is <gloss>44/7</gloss>. Adding the half-multiplier <gloss>40/7</gloss> and squaring the result, the total number of swans is produced: 144.

**Explanation:** Following the rule mentioned in the second verse, we subtract the eighth part <gloss>1/8</gloss> from one. Thus <gloss>1/1 - 1/8</gloss> equals <gloss>7/8</gloss>. When the visible quantity 6 is divided by this, <gloss>6/1 ÷ 7/8</gloss> = <gloss>6/1 × 8/7</gloss> = <gloss>48/7</gloss>. After performing the transformation <note>clarification: to a common denominator</note>, <gloss>48/7</gloss> becomes the visible quantity. Similarly, when the square root multiplier 10 is divided by <gloss>7/8</gloss>, <gloss>10/1 ÷ 7/8</gloss> = <gloss>10/1 × 8/7</gloss> = <gloss>80/7</gloss>. By performing the transformation, <gloss>80/7</gloss> becomes the square root multiplier. Now, taking <gloss>48/7</gloss> as the visible quantity and <gloss>80/7</gloss> as the square root multiplier, the operation is performed according to the method stated in the previous verse. That is, half of the square root multiplier is <gloss>40/7</gloss>. After squaring <gloss>40/7</gloss>, it becomes <gloss>1600/49</gloss>. Adding this to the visible quantity <gloss>48/7</gloss>...

III. First, it is evident that a possessor in <term>bona fide</term> <gloss>good faith</gloss> (for a possessor in bad faith is held liable beyond the value of the thing due to his own action) is not held liable for any restitution if the thing has perished, because he neither has the thing itself, nor any profit from the thing.

<margin>Medina de contr. q. 10. Zeff. l. II. c. 14. Navar. c. 17. n. 7.</margin>
IV. Secondly, a possessor in good faith is held liable to restore even the existing fruits of the thing. I say the fruits of the thing; for the fruits of industry, even if they would not have been produced without the thing, are nevertheless not owed to the thing. The cause of this obligation is from ownership; for he who is the owner of the thing is also naturally the owner of the fruits of the thing.

V. Thirdly, a possessor in good faith is held liable for the restitution of both the thing and the consumed fruits, provided that he would otherwise have consumed just as much; for in this he is considered enriched. Thus, Gaius Caesar Caligula <margin>Suet. c. 16.</margin> is praised in the beginnings of his reign because, to those to whom he restored kingdoms, he also added the fruits of the intervening time.

VI. Fourthly, he is not held liable for fruits which he neglected to gather, because he has neither the thing, nor anything that succeeds in the place of the thing.

VII. Fifthly, if such a possessor gives to another a thing donated to him, he is not held liable unless he would have donated just as much even without this thing; for then it will be a profit to have spared his own property.

<margin>L. Quivaes. §. ult. D. furti.</margin>
VIII. Sixthly, if he has sold a thing he bought, he is not held liable, unless perhaps to the extent that he sold it for more. But if he sold a donated thing, he is held liable to restore the price, unless perhaps he squandered the price, which he would not otherwise have squandered.

<margin>L. fi & rem. D. de petit. hereditatis. L. Sed & si lege. D. eod. L. Si eum servum. D. de rebus creditis. L. Mater tua. L. Si mancipia. D. de rei vindicatione.</margin>
IX. Seventhly, a thing of another bought in good faith must be restored, nor can the price paid be reclaimed. To this rule, in my opinion, this exception should be added: unless the owner could not reasonably have recovered possession of his property without some expenditure, as for instance if the thing had been with pirates. For then, the amount that the owner would have gladly spent can be deducted. For the possession of the fact itself, especially when difficult to recover, is something estimable, and in this, the owner is considered to have been enriched after the loss of the thing. And therefore, although the purchase of one's own property is not valid under ordinary law, Paulus the jurist says it is valid if it was agreed from the beginning that the possession which is with another should be purchased. Nor do I require here that the thing be bought with the intention that it be restored to the owner, in which case there are those who say that an action for the management of affairs arises.

<margin>L. Sucr. D. de cont. emt. L. 1. D. de evittionibus. L. Si laborav. §. Si navis. D. ad legem Rhodiam. pern. v. quid de praedam ementibus. Aegid. Reg. diff. 35. dub. 7. num. 126. Host. tit. de a L. Si in emtione §. rei. D. de contr. emt.</margin>

...Christians, he <note>context: Celsus, the second-century critic of Christianity.</note> says that the Jews were fugitives from Egypt who never performed anything noteworthy, and were never of any account either in reputation or in number. Now, concerning the fact that they were not fugitives, nor Egyptians, but Hebrews who had settled in Egypt, we have already spoken in the preceding sections. If he thinks he can establish that they were of no account in reputation or number from the fact that their history is hardly found among the Greeks, we shall say this: if anyone were to dwell upon their original constitution and the arrangement of their laws, he would find that they were people displaying a shadow of heavenly life on earth. Among them, no other was recognized as God than the one over all, and no maker of images lived as a citizen. For there was neither painter nor sculptor in their commonwealth, since the law expelled all such people from it, so that there would be no pretext for the construction of images, which attracts the attention of foolish men and drags the eyes of the soul down from God to the earth. There was also such a law among them: "Do not act lawlessly and make for yourselves a carved likeness, any image of the likeness of male or female, the likeness of any beast that is on the earth, the likeness of any winged bird that flies under heaven, the likeness of any creeping thing that creeps on the earth, the likeness of any fish, as many as are in the waters under the earth." <note>context: Deuteronomy 4:16–18.</note> And the law certainly intended that they, by communing with the truth of each thing, should not fashion other things contrary to the truth, which give a false representation of the truly male, or the real female, or the nature of beasts, or the genus of birds, or of creeping things, or of fish. <meta>This page contains commentaries on Chapter 48 and the beginning of Chapter 49 of the Tao Te Ching. The commentaries are attributed to Su Che, Lu Huiqing, Huang Maocai, and Xi Zhai.</meta>

<margin>Commentary by Su <note>context: Su Che (1039–1112), a prominent Song dynasty statesman and scholar.</note></margin> One who does not know the Way <term>Tao</term> and yet devotes himself to learning will find that what he hears and sees increases daily. If he has no means to unify this knowledge, it inevitably becomes a burden. Confucius said: "Hear much, select what is good and follow it; see much and remember it; this is the second level of knowledge." If one day a person comes to know the Way, they will look back on their former pretenses and artificial actions as entirely false. By removing the false and returning to one's true nature, this is called "decreasing." Confucius said to Zigong: "Do you think I am one who learns many things and remembers them?" Zigong replied: "Yes, is it not so?" Confucius said: "No, I pervade them all with a single thread." When the mind is forgotten in order to return purely to nature, this is called "decreasing." Yet as long as any trace of falseness remains, one must continue until even this forgetting is forgotten, and the nature is restored without residue. Then one moves beyond action <term>wei</term> and does not fail to reach non-action <term>wu wei</term>. All people have desires and a mind that seeks to take hold of the world and its affairs. Therefore, when they initiate actions and seek results, their intentions are visible externally, and things resist them; thus, they meet difficulties and fail. The Sage practices non-action and therefore has no "affairs" in his mind. This is visible externally, and things are at peace with him. Though he does not seek to take the world or manage its affairs, the world and its affairs naturally settle into order through him.

<margin>Commentary by Lu <note>context: Lu Huiqing (1035–1111), a high-ranking official and reformer of the Northern Song dynasty.</note></margin> Engaging in learning <term>wei xue</term> is for those who have not yet heard the Way. When one seeks what has not been heard, one cannot help but be broad; thus it is said to "increase daily." Engaging in the Way <term>wei tao</term> is for those who have already heard the Way. Once it is heard, one cannot help but practice non-action; thus it is said to "decrease daily." To "decrease and further decrease" implies that one has not yet escaped the realm of purposeful action. Only by decreasing the "decreaser" itself does one reach non-action. Non-action means to be still and unmoving. "Nothing left undone" means that when stimulated, one penetrates all the causes under heaven. Reaching non-action through the process of non-action is what is called the Constant. Learning without worry is called spirit. The direction of the spirit is what is called the Way. Who but the most spiritual can attain this? From this we see that taking the world is always done through non-action. As for using purposeful action, it is clear that such is insufficient to take the world.

<column-break/>

<margin>Commentary by Huang Maocai</margin> Only after knowing everything can one speak of learning; therefore, learning seeks daily increase. Only after reaching a state where nothing is done for a purpose can one speak of the Way; therefore, the Way seeks daily decrease. That which increases can be sought through progress, but that which decreases is sometimes difficult to achieve through forceful effort. Only the most enlightened can suddenly cast everything off and reach the realm of non-action. Thus, they can do everything, and their practical application is inexhaustible, acting upon the world with effortless ease.

<margin>Commentary by Xi Zhai</margin> Engaging in learning is the means to seek knowledge, thus it increases daily. Engaging in the Way is the means to remove the false, thus it decreases daily. If knowledge is not perfected, the decreasing will not be complete; therefore, daily increase provides the ground for daily decrease. If one decreases and further decreases until the false is gone and the true is whole, then one reaches non-action. Once non-action is reached, then every purposeful action is essentially non-action; this is something that cannot easily be discussed in terms of mere "increase" or "decrease." When non-action reaches its peak, though the things of the world are many, they are unified by a single thread. If one attempts to handle the world through purposeful interference, even a single object creates entanglement and error; how much worse would it be with the vastness of the world?

The Sage has no fixed mind; he takes the mind of the people as his own. To those who are good, I am good. To those who are not good, I am also good; thus virtue is goodness. To those who are trustful, I trust them. To those who are not trustful, I also trust them; thus virtue is trust. The Sage dwells in the world with a blurred and settled mind, making the mind of the world muddy and undifferentiated. The people all focus their ears and eyes upon him; the Sage <unclear>treats them all as children</unclear>.

Sacrifice a pure maiden to the gods below,
One chosen by lot from the blood of the Aepytidae.
Perform your holy rites with nightly slaughters.
But if she who is sacrificed belongs to another, then
Let him sacrifice, giving his own for slaughter willingly.

When the god revealed this, they immediately cast lots for all the maidens of the lineage of the Aepytidae. The lot fell upon the daughter of Lyciscus. But Epebolus the seer forbade them to sacrifice her, claiming she was not actually the child of Lyciscus; he said the woman who lived with Lyciscus was unable to bear children and had secretly substituted the girl. While the seer was explaining these details, Lyciscus took the girl and deserted to Sparta. When the Messenians fell into despair upon learning that Lyciscus had fled, a man named Aristodemus, who was also of the race of the Aepytidae and was more distinguished than Lyciscus both in general reputation and in matters of war, offered his own daughter to be sacrificed willingly.

However, destiny often conceals human zeal in such matters, just as a pebble is hidden by the mud of a river. Even then, as Aristodemus strove to save the Messenians, destiny brought the following obstacle. A certain man of the Messenians (whose name they do not record) happened to be in love with the daughter of Aristodemus. At that time, he was already about to take her as his wife. Initially, he entered into a dispute with Aristodemus, arguing that since Aristodemus had betrothed her to him, he was no longer the master of the girl, but that he himself, as the betrothed, had greater authority over her. Secondly, when he saw that this was not succeeding, he turned to a shameful argument, claiming that he had slept with the girl and that she was pregnant by him. Finally, he provoked Aristodemus to such an extent that, driven mad by rage, he killed his daughter. Afterwards, he cut her open and demonstrated that she was not with child.

Epebolus, who was present, then ordered that someone else must give up a daughter; for he said that the death of Aristodemus's daughter achieved nothing for them, as her father had murdered her rather than sacrificing her to the gods commanded by the Pythia. When the seer said this, the mass of the Messenians rushed to kill the girl’s suitor, believing he had brought a useless pollution upon Aristodemus and had made their hope of salvation uncertain. But this man was a very close friend to Euphaes. Euphaes persuaded the Messenians that the oracle had been fulfilled by the girl’s death and that what Aristodemus had done was sufficient for them. When he said this, all those of the Aepytidae lineage agreed that he spoke the truth; for their own fear for their daughters was ended, and each man hurried away. The kings, persuaded by this advice, dismissed the assembly, and from there they turned to sacrifices and a festival of the gods.

When the Lacedaemonians <note>context: The Spartans.</note> heard of the oracle given to the Messenians, they and their kings also became disheartened, hesitant to engage in battle or take any further action. In the sixth year after Lyciscus fled from Ithome, the Lacedaemonians—since their omens had become favorable—marched against Ithome. The Cretans happened to no longer be present with them. The allies of the Messenians were also late. For the Spartans were already viewed with suspicion by the other Peloponnesians, especially the Arcadians and Argives. The Argives intended to arrive secretly from the Lacedaemonians, and specifically as individuals rather than by a common decree. The Arcadians had been openly forbidden from the expedition. Thus, they too were not present.

The reputation of the oracle led the Messenians to risk battle even without allies. For the most part, the engagement was no different from the previous battle; on that day, too, the light failed while they were still fighting. They do not record that either wing or any company was forced back. For they say that they did not remain in the ranks as they were originally stationed, but the best men from both sides met in the center, and there the whole weight of the struggle took place. Euphaes, showing more spirit than was expected of a king, pressed recklessly against those around Theopompus, receiving many wounds, some of them fatal. Fainting from loss of blood...
